en: Upon entering the assembly, one must know the circumstances for sitting in meditation, entering the room to seek instruction,
and the ritual of announcing the incense offering.
Format for the Tea Service during the New and Full Moon Rounds of the Hall and the Quarters; Small Sermons on the New and Full Moon Days when Ascending the Hall,
and the Five-Day Sessions of Ascending the Hall and Holding the Whisk.
Upon entering the *danguo* (overnight guest quarters), one meets the *zhike* (guest master) to request the hanging of the *da* (certificate of ordination);

one meets the *shizhe* (attendant) to request the advancement or dismissal of the *toushou* (heads of departments); one requests the advancement or dismissal of the *zhishi* (administrative officers); and one requests the appointment of *shizhe*.
The Form for the Special Tea Service for Newly Arrived Monks Prior to Summer Retreat;
The Form for the Request for Tea for Newly Arrived Monks by the Head Seat Prior to Summer Retreat;
The Official Note for the Special Tea Service for Newly Arrived Monks Prior to Summer Retreat; The Ritual for the Unbinding of Karmic Ties and Social Greetings.
The Special Tea Service for the Abbot;
the Special Tea Service for the Head Seat; the Special Tea Service for the Assistant Seat;
the Form for the Tea and Soup Signboard; and the Form of the Request for Tea by the Head Seat.
The Form for the Treasury Office’s Announcement on Medicines; The Form for the Abbot’s Announcement Exempting Guests from Formal Visits;
The Form for Requesting a Seat upon Meeting with Monks of Various Mountains;
The Rules for the Bell and Drum; The Special Envoy’s Request for the Abbot to Take Office.

Submission of the Seal and Presentation of the Ordination Certificate (contained within).
The Format for the Notification of Death and the Announcement of the Passing of the Abbot upon Receipt of a Letter from Afar.
Formal Memorial Letter for the Venerable Jieshi:
Notice for the Monastic Assembly regarding the offering of incense, the commencement of the rites,
and the conclusion of the ceremonies for the Buddha’s Bathing, His Enlightenment, and His Parinirvāṇa.

The Ritual for the Summer Retreat Recitation; the Ritual for the Conclusion of the Retreat; the Ritual for Offerings on the Emperor’s Birthday; the Ritual for the New Year’s Eve; the Ritual for the Anniversary of the Patriarchs’ Death;
the Ritual for the Recitation for Ill Monks; the Ritual for the Great Night of Senior Dignitaries.
Regarding the chanting of robes and recitations:

the imperial decree does not permit disturbances during such matters as the regular chanting for the distribution of robes or for deceased monks (from the *Jintang ji*). [The stele is located at] Jingxiu Dongchan Xiufeng Zongchengtian.
The Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras: Instructions for Novices.
Instructions for Donors Sending Off the Deceased, Continuing the Lineage, Receiving the Full Ordination, Returning to the Hall,
and Joining the Assembly.
Regarding the method for entering the assembly: do not fall asleep before [the others], nor wake up after them. At the first watch (one *diǎn*) of the second watch, set aside your pillow.

At the fifth *diǎn* of the third watch, rise. Place your pillow at the foot of the bed without folding it, fearing that it might make a noise. If you become weary while sitting, push the quilt back under your feet.
Placing the hand-towel over his hands, he descended from the bed and recited this verse:
I am three feet from the ground, Yet I imagine you standing before me; Should I inadvertently tread upon you, May you be swiftly reborn in heaven.

An ancient saying goes: When lifting the curtain, move your hands lightly; when exiting the hall, avoid wearing slippers. Take only a small amount of hot water and a small amount of tooth-cleansing powder;

do not take more than necessary, for fear that those who follow might catch "tooth-wind" (dental ailments) or be splashed by spit. When spitting water, one must keep the head low. One must not make noise while rinsing or washing the mouth.
One must not wash one's hair, as it soils the towel, soils the bucket, causes the hair to become brittle, and damages the eyes—these are the four disadvantages. Return to the hall.
In the upper section of the hall, enter first with the left foot; in the lower section, enter first with the right foot. Return to your assigned seat. When taking up your bedding, fold it in half.
Once seated, if you wish to change your *zhiduo* (straight robe), first cover your head and body before changing; do not expose your bare skin or fan yourself.
Before the bell has sounded, some may go privately to pay homage to the Buddha; they should simply take their *kāṣāya* out of the hall, but must not put it on before leaving.
Once it is donned, they should join their palms at the crown of their head. The verse says:
Excellent is the robe of liberation, the signless field-of-merit garment. Now I receive it upon my head; may I wear it constantly throughout all lifetimes.
*Oṃ siddhye svāhā.* Fold the *kāṣāya* [robe].
Do not hold it in the mouth or hook it under the chin. Once folded, perform a formal greeting (*praṇāma*). It is improper to burn incense as one would in a hall or temple.
Stand in the center to perform prostrations; this is the position for the abbot. When performing the circumambulation (*xíngdào*), one must not pass in front of others while they are prostrating.

When the bell tolls, one may not enter or exit through the hall doors. Once the bell has ceased and the bedding has been folded, wait until the small purification board (*xiǎojìngbǎn*) sounds before entering or exiting.
When the bell has ceased and the bedding is folded, and the small purification board sounds, fold the pillow. First find its two corners and tuck them inside the bedding.

Fearing noise, when folding the bedding, one must straighten the body and seek out both corners to fold them; it is not permitted to fold by spreading them out horizontally, as this would create a draft that interferes with the continuous mats.

When the signal for great silence (*dàjìng*) sounds and the fire-bell (*huólíng*) passes, return to your bowl-position and sit. Enter through the side of the guest door at the front of the hall, always leading with the left foot;
do not walk through the center, as that is reserved for the Abbot. When the wooden fish (*mùyú*) sounds, you must not enter.

The Hall. When entering the hall, one should walk slowly and with measured steps. Upon reaching one’s seat for the alms bowl, turn the body in accordance with the direction of the *kāṣāya*; do not turn so as to have one’s back toward it.

Ascend the platform and sit in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), ensuring that no part of the body is exposed. Do not converse with those seated beside you while holding the bowl. Upon hearing the long board strike, descend from the platform with the bowl.
With one hand holding the alms bowl and the other hand unhooking it, he crouches down to set it down. When the bell tolls before the hall, he descends from his seat and performs a formal greeting;
this is the reception of the abbot. When the mallet sounds, he spreads out his bowl and recites the verse:

"The Tathāgata is the worthy vessel; now that I have been granted this opportunity, may I, together with all sentient beings, realize the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres, and only then remove my robes.
He spreads his cloth over his knees, folds it into a triangle, and places the bowl-cloth, folded, upon the single-layered robe by his side.

Place the spoon upon the chopsticks. When entering, the spoon comes first; when departing, the chopsticks follow last. Once the *vinaya-dhara* has struck the gavel, the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) offers the food.
There are ten benefits to gruel: it greatly benefits the practitioner, resulting in boundless retribution and ultimate, eternal bliss.

At the time of the midday meal, with the three virtues and six flavors, one makes offerings to the Buddha, the Sangha, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, universally providing for them all. As for the ten benefits: (1) gathering the assembly; (2) ...

Joy; three types of faith; four types of diligence; five types of thirst-quenching; six types of shame and remorse; seven types of producing goodness; eight types of pleasant sound; nine types of having form; ten types of sustaining the body. Three virtues: (1) lightness and softness; (2) purity and cleanliness;

(3) accordance with the Dharma. Six flavors: sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, sour, and bland. If it is on the first or fifteenth day of the month, once the *vina* has struck the meal gong throughout the hall, he returns to face the *shouzuo* (head seat), bows from a distance once, and then returns to his own place.
He strikes the gong once more to request the offering of wealth, and the *shouzuo* makes the offering.
Master Cai said: "The two kinds of giving—of material wealth and of the Dharma—are equal and without distinction; thus, the *dānapāramitā* is fully perfected.

When it comes to the ritual of offering incense, the attendant distributes the undergarments (*cīvara*). The practitioner first performs the salutation, and the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) subsequently distributes the undergarments. The verse for when the monastic community receives food says:
When receiving food, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings: "May they take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance, and may they be filled with the delight of the Dharma.

Next, perform the five contemplations: 1. Calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from which it was brought. 2. Reflect upon whether your own virtue and conduct are complete or deficient, considering that you may not deserve such offerings.
3. Guard the mind against transgressions, taking the subduing of greed and other afflictions as the primary aim. 4. Regard the food as excellent medicine intended to cure illness.
The body becomes withered. Fifth, one shall receive this food only after accomplishing the work of the Path. A verse of birth says:
"O you hosts of ghosts and spirits, I now bestow upon you this offering; may this food reach all ghosts and spirits throughout the ten directions."
Regarding the method of eating: one should bring the food to the mouth, not the mouth to the food. When taking up or setting down the bowl, one must not make a sound, nor should one cough.
One should receive food according to one's need to avoid requesting more; until one has requested more, one must not rinse the bowl.
One must not wash the bowl with hot water. One must not pour out the residual water.
Before the water has been poured out, one must not fold and store the knee-cloth. The verse on pouring out the water says:
This water from my broken bowl Has a flavor like celestial nectar;
I universally bestow it upon all spirits and ghosts, Causing them all to be fully satiated. Oṃ maheśvara-svāhā.

[Having finished reciting the scripture after rising from the hall, the board for the quarters sounds. Return to the quarters. Attend the assembly for greetings. One must not leave while reading the scriptures.]
Regarding the sound: before the meditation board has even been struck, one must first loosen the belt; do not wait until the last moment to act in haste.

One may place a clean cloth over the left hand and fasten the belt upon it, tying it straight and neat so that it is perfectly aligned. With the right hand holding the bucket, enter the latrine with shoes placed level and upright.
Once the clean bucket has been set down, snap the fingers three times to startle away the dung-eating spirits. One must squat with the body perfectly upright; it must not be slanted.
Regarding nasal mucus and saliva: when the door is closed and bolted, one should merely snap the fingers lightly; it cannot be endured for people to make a chaotic noise.

When entering, use a tally-stick (śalākā), which must touch the pure area. When exiting, one must avoid leaving water tracks across the floor. Wash with the left hand, protecting the thumb and the second finger.
One must not use too many counting-sticks (*śalākā*). An ancient saying states: "Use little bath-water and let the sticks be lightly moistened; this is one way of cherishing merit.

After picking up ash with the right hand, pick up earth next, and then use soap-nuts (*kappūra*) to wash the hands. One must recite the mantras for entering the latrine and washing clean. An ancient saying states:
"If one does not recite the mantras when washing clean, even if one were to wash with all the waters of the great ocean, it would only reach as far as the vajra-base."
The edges [of the robe] likewise cannot be purified. Just as one may not don the *kāṣāya* or read the scriptures without having washed them clean, so too for entering the latrine:
the mantra is *Oṃ huluḍāya svāhā*.
For washing: Oṃ hana amṛte svāhā. For washing the hands: Oṃ jugalaye svāhā.
For purifying the body: Oṃ śrīye mahi svāhā.
To remove impurities, recite: *Oṃ vajranakhāṭa svāhā*. One must use water for rinsing the mouth.
Before the midday meal and after the evening meal, it is not permitted to open chests or cabinets. If there is an urgent matter, one must inform the head of the administrative office (*liáozhǔ*).

Within the hall, one must inform the attendant of the Holy Sangha (*shèngsēng shìzhě*). A space of three feet in front of the bed is considered pure. First, unfold the alms bowl; second, unfold the *kāṣāya* robe.
Face the three directions. After the midday meal, you must wear the *kaishi* (waistband). You must not go barefoot or wear shoes. As the ancients said:
"Walk with measured steps, emulating the majestic deportment of Aśvajit; speak in a low voice, following the model of Upāli. One must not tilt the hot water pitcher to soak clothes.
Personal documents, once used, must be returned to their original place so as not to hinder others' use. Sit in meditation in the evening.

Small Sermon. The bell rings and the session is dismissed. The assembly bows in unison (*vaṃdanā*). The meditation mats are folded and half-removed. If it is a Great Sermon (*mahā-kathā*), one should first inform the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) in advance;

a signboard is hung at the communal quarters stating: "Tonight, sit in the hall. The communal quarters strike the wooden board, and only then does the Abbot and the Head Seat enter the hall to take their seats.
Once the board in front of the Head Seat’s quarters is struck, the entire assembly turns as one, and the Head Seat then descends from his position.
At the ground, burn one stick of incense. Return once more to your original position and sit firmly. The practice leader (xingzhe) covers and lowers the *can-zhang* (the screen).

Afterward, the attendant who calls for the meal stands first by the side of the *can-yi* (the practice chair) and calls for the lowering of the *can*. Three strikes of the bell are sounded in the hall;

each person performs a *wande* (greeting) and exits with half their mat, as is the same as during the *xiaocan* (small lecture). In the evening, return to the hall at the proper time; do not wait for the striking of the bell in front of the quarters.
Emerging from the quarters, the evening bell tolls. Joining the palms, one recites the verse:
Hearing this sound of the bell, one transcends the Dharma-realm; The dark obscurity of the Iron Ring Mountains is entirely illuminated.
The agonies of the three miserable realms and eight difficulties are all stilled; May all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment.

Return to your place and sit in meditation. You are not permitted to rise before the bell for the end of the period has struck. Only when the fire-bell sounds may you go outside to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) or perform prostrations in secret.
When sleeping, you must lie on your right side; you must not lie on your back, as that is the "corpse sleep. After the bell for the end of the period has struck—

Remove the *kāṣāya* and wrap it in a *saṃkakṣikā*, then place it upon the chest of the storage cabinet. Next is the method for entering the bathhouse: drape a hand towel over the left hand and hold bathing implements with the right hand.
Enter the lower section and perform a formal greeting (*praṇāma*). Those of seniority occupy the upper section, while those of junior standing occupy the lower section.
Then, unfold the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), wrap the foot-cloth around the body, put on the bathing skirt, take up the undergarment, and first lay out the outer robe.
Inside, take the *zhiduō* (straight robe) and hang it on the rack. Before removing your undergarments, you must not yet take off the *zhiduō*.
You must not enter the bath barefoot. You must not occupy the seat of honor. You may gently take the hot water, taking care not to splash anyone.
If you rise to take the water, you must wrap your lower garment around your legs. When leaving the bath, first put on your upper garment. [Question: What next?
Upon exiting the hall, one should form this thought: "May all sentient beings together attain complete purity. Then recite the Heart Sutra as a response to the benefactor.
Regarding items such as the public notice board, incense spoons, and fire tongs, one must not handle them playfully. If an item is found, it should be hung on the "Lost and Found" board.
One may also clean small signs. When shaving the head, one must follow the prescribed order. In matters of the hearth, yield to those who are senior and experienced.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one should always look toward the higher stream. By being entirely humble and respectful, one will naturally be free from error.
One should peruse the ancient texts on pure regulations (*qinggui*), the verses of the various patriarchs, the essential compendium for beginners, and the precious instructions of the Chan school.
Through such practice and study, one may reflect upon oneself (as detailed in the *Wuliang xuzhi*).

Regarding daily *zazen*: the attendant of the Hall Office reports to the Abbot and the Head Seat; then he strikes the board in front of the various quarters three times and strikes the board in front of the Meditation Hall.
Once the assembly of monks has entered the hall and taken their seats, he strikes the board in front of the Head Seat’s quarters three times for each.
The Head Seat enters the hall to burn incense and makes one circuit of the hall. As soon as the fire-board sounds, the Head Seat rises first, while the rest of the assembly may act as they please.
After the midday meal, they prepare for practice, sitting in meditation at will. They sit in meditation during the fourth watch; see the "Section on Joining the Assembly" for details.

At the striking of the dusk bell, they enter the hall. At the striking of the fixed bell, they rise to relieve themselves. Reaching two points past the second watch, they remove their pillows and rest. When the dusk bell rings, the assembly...
When a person enters the hall, the first stroke of the bell is struck. When the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) enters the hall, the third stroke of the bell is struck.
Only when the bell has ceased does the circumambulation of the hall begin. If the Abbot has not yet arrived or is absent, the Head Seat shall perform the circumambulation.

During the fourth watch, the Head Seat circumambulates first, followed by the arrival of the Abbot for the circumambulation. For those practicing "Dry Zen" (Kuchan), the sitting board is not struck; they should instead constantly cultivate ultimate realization throughout the day.
For three nights, one should gather and collect the body and mind to thoroughly penetrate the Great Matter.

Regarding the practice of entering the room for three days and eight nights, this is the established rule for the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*); alternatively, it may not be restricted by specific times or seasons. When the drum is struck three times, the Abbot enters his quarters.
The assembly sits inside. The attendant offers greetings and stands in a row outside the room on the side of the master. A kneeling mat is placed outside the threshold.
Each member of the assembly takes a small incense case with a stick of incense and, proceeding to the large incense burner, performs three full prostrations; do not occupy the center.
Next, they stand in a formation like a flight of geese and proceed gradually toward the west. Seniority in precepts is not taken into account; whoever arrives first takes the lead.

If a *zhishi* (administrative official) or a *doushou* (head of a department) arrives later, it is permissible for them to join the front ranks. Upon entering the gate, one first steps with the left foot. Facing the abbot, one performs a formal greeting (*wenshen*).
Turning toward the southwest corner of the meditation chair, one stands with hands crossed, awaiting the abbot to pose a question. Or...

Having spoken the lower words—or not speaking them—he returns once more to the center to inquire after [the master’s] well-being. Turning his body and joining his palms, he exits from the eastern side.
First raising his left foot, he steps outside the door, performs a prostration by touching the ground, and returns to the hall for investigation.
Requesting Instruction:
Tonight, I wish to go to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to request instruction. In the evening, I first informed the Attendant (shizhe), who conveyed my request to the Abbot with his approval.

After the *dingzhong* bell has struck, I shall go to the Attendants’ Office (shisi) and proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters to request instruction. Having lit incense and performed nine prostrations, I say: "The matter of birth and death is great; I hope you will grant me your guidance."

The Master revealed the essential points of the Dharma. [The disciples] stood to one side and listened attentively. Once the instruction was finished, they again burned incense, performed three prostrations with touching of the forehead, and withdrew.

Regarding new arrivals who have registered for the summer retreat and wish to seek entry into the master’s room to request further instruction, the head of the quarters should consult with them in advance.
The council deliberated on the matter. On one day, the head of the assembly went to the Attendant’s Office and said, "Brothers who have newly returned to the hall wish to offer incense;
please trouble the attendant to announce this to the Abbot for his consideration. Once permission was granted, he immediately informed the community.

He recruited three contributors for the incense fund and, having prepared the diagrams in advance, they practiced the ritual procedures. They arranged the space in the Dharma Hall, setting out three incense burners in a single row and establishing the place for prostration.

Regarding the general discourse for the hanging of the meditation mat (*zuo-xi*): use small slips of paper with the characters "Gaoxiang" (Announcement of Incense) written on them and affix them to the quarters of the senior monks.
Strike the wooden board three times to assemble the assembly; count how many people there are and arrange them into several rows, standing facing east and west.

Designate a head participant (*can-tou*) to stand in the center and bow upon the meditation mat, then temporarily leave his position and, together with the attendant, go to the upper hall to invite the Abbot to emerge.

Once they have taken their seats, the head of the assembly (sanzu) returns to his position and bows in greeting. He alone burns a single stick of incense, returns to his position, and performs three full prostrations with the sitting cloth fully spread.
Rising from his seat, the head of the assembly approaches the abbot, bows in greeting, turns to stand at a slight angle in the southwest corner, and says:
"The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. We humbly pray that the Venerable Master will grant us an instruction on the causes and conditions. The abbot then speaks.

[The Master] speaks. The head of the assembly responds with three turning-words and returns to his position. Again, a large incense stick is burned. [The participants] return to their original positions and stand.
In succession, the assembly from the east and west proceeds out in two rows to burn incense. Each follows the diagram for coming and going:

they exit from the front with hands in the *añjali* (crossed) gesture and return from the rear with palms joined (*añjali*). Three people form one group; six people on each side are divided into three groups for the incense burners.
Incense is burned. Two persons attend each incense burner; when offering the initial incense, they both proceed from the center.

After exiting to the front of the burners and finishing the burning of the incense, one person stands behind the burner while the other remains in the center. Both sides of the burner are treated in this same manner.

Once the incense has been burned evenly by all, each performs three full prostrations. Rising, they do not fold their sitting cloths (*zuoju*). The head of the assembly (*candou*) bows deeply to inquire after the well-being of the assembly, then joins his palms and says: "I humbly hope..."
"Out of your great compassion, Master, you have graciously bestowed this instruction. Your humble servant is moved by a sense of profound gratitude beyond measure.
He then withdrew and performed three prostrations. The attendant directed the acolytes to strike the drum five times. The assembly divided into east and west, standing facing one another.

Next, the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and heads of departments (*tou-shou*) emerged and took their places in the ranks. The Abbot delivered a general discourse (*pushe*). When the discourse was concluded, the administrative officers...

The head monk withdraws. The assembly stands according to their positions. The lead participant returns to the center, burns another piece of incense, and returns to his original place with the assembly.

Again, they perform three full prostrations without folding the sitting cloth (*zuoju*). Stepping forward, he says: "We, [Name] and others, have been fortunate in past lives to have already received the Compassionate Master’s instruction on the essentials of the Dharma.
Our humble hearts are filled with boundless joy. He then withdraws and performs another three prostrations.

He bows and says, "On this day, I humbly wish that you may enjoy ten thousand blessings. He then withdraws three paces, bows again, folds his sitting mat, rises, and makes an inquiry before withdrawing.
When the assembly reaches the Dharma Hall, they bow once to thank the attendant and then bow once to thank the head of the assembly. After the meal is finished:
The Abbot specifically prepares tea for the assembly and invites the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to accompany him.

Whether it be for a newly admitted monk to offer incense (*gāoxiang*) or for a monk who has been invited from elsewhere to ascend the hall and deliver a discourse (*shuōle*), upon descending from the seat, he joins the assembly in bowing and making the invitation. Next, there is the invitation for further instruction (*qǐyì*) and the offering of incense for a general discourse (*pǔshuō*).

Sometimes this takes place in the Hall of Illumination (*Zhàotáng*); in some places, there is a "Great Zen Session" (*Dàcān*). At that point, the board is struck in the hall, and the head of the retreat (*Cāntóu*) delivers a general discourse to conclude the session. Thereafter...
When the Zhaotang Hall opens its quarters, the ceremonial protocol is the same as that for previously entering the quarters.

If the guest is a person of renowned virtue, such as a West Hall Head Seat or a senior monk (zunsu), the abbot should have an attendant deliver a message in advance, saying: "Please do not trouble yourself to descend from your dignity. It would be improper to dismiss them with a shout.

As for the ritual of announcing the incense (gaoxiang), it is for the host to perform; alternatively, one may offer a prostration with hands touching the ground (chuli) to express gratitude. Furthermore, this may also be done after the announcement of the incense has concluded.
At one's convenience, strike the drum and enter the hall. After three days have passed, the Abbot shall invite the assembly for the medicinal meal (*yao-shi*) and provide offerings as appropriate.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, conduct the inspection of the hall.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, he ascends the hall. Taking his seat, he says: "Descend from the seat to tour the hall for tea.

The Head Seat leads the assembly, touring the hall once according to the prescribed diagram, standing at the primary position. The Abbot enters the hall, burns incense, and returns to his place; the administrative officers form a single row.
The Abbot enters the hall to pay his respects to the Sangha. The Rector (Zhuchi) makes one circuit of the hall.

If he has arrived only temporarily, he first joins the assembly and subsequently stands behind the curtain with the Attendant (Shizhe). When the administrators (Zhishi) are about to leave the hall, he follows them out.

Once the Attendant returns to the hall, and after the usual incense burning and tea service are completed, the bowls are collected and the "Retreat from Hall" bell is struck three times. If there is no formal circuit of the hall, it is simply the morning gruel.
The session ends. Take their seats to drink tea. The three [officers] patrol the hall; what was seen previously need not be recorded again.
They patrol the quarters (starting from the east).

A "Patrolling the Quarters" plaque is hung above the hall, and small plaques are hung in each of the various quarters. Incense tables, candles, and other items must be arranged accordingly. Care must be taken to ensure...
[The assembly] stands in formation. When the Abbot approaches the Head of the Quarters (Liaozhu), he presents the items for the Head of the Quarters and escorts him out of his own quarters.
The assembly lines up before the quarters and stands waiting until the Abbot passes; they then follow behind him with palms joined.

As they pass through each of the other quarters in turn, once all have been completed, the Abbot stands before the Dharma Hall. When the assembly has passed by three people [in depth], they perform a single "upward-turning" bow (*shang zhuan shen*) and inquire after his well-being.
Carry this to the various quarters for the personnel matters. The message states: "We humbly receive the honor of the Master’s visit;

our hearts are filled with profound gratitude. We need not discuss the warmth of the season. Once the rounds of the quarters are completed, the attendant instructs the acolytes to prepare embroidered tea banners, broken tea, and incense.
They proceed to the Head Seat’s quarters, burn incense, and request the time for the meal. Specifically, the tea banners are posted on the upper section of the hall in front of the building.

The Format for the Tea Service Announcement: This morning, following the midday meal, the Abbot shall proceed to the Cloud Hall to serve one round of tea specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly, briefly to commemorate [the commencement of the retreat, the conclusion of the retreat, a seasonal festival, or the New Year; alternatively, it may be called a "presentation of congratulations"].
Regarding the protocol for the venerable person [Name]: We respectfully request that all the administrative officers likewise deign to attend as honored companions. This would be most fortunate.
On this day of this month, [Name] of the Attendant Office respectfully informs you.

On the evening of the first day of the new moon or full moon, when it is time for the *shàngtáng* (ascending the hall), the attendant informs the abbot. The following morning, the notice board is hung, and the attendants are ordered to notify all the quarters.
The first drum is struck, and the Head Seat leads the assembly into the hall. At the second drum, they exit the hall; at the third drum, the attendant [prepares for the next proceedings].
Waiting for the assembly to gather, he performs a single inquiry (wèn-xùn). Turning his body, he receives the Abbot and ascends the Dharma seat together with him to stand in attendance.

He holds up the incense box. The Abbot takes up the incense and offers prayers for the Emperor. Once the prayers for the Emperor are concluded, the attendant receives the incense, arranges it within the burner, and the Abbot descends from the seat.
Once the abbot has taken his seat, the attendant (shizhe) steps out of the ranks and first performs a greeting (wenshen). Next, the two classes of monks do so;
the western class first departs from their primary seats and moves to the center to greet, while the eastern class departs from their junior seats to greet.

The attendant then ascends the Dharma seat as originally prescribed, holding incense in his left hand, turns his body to perform a greeting, and the abbot requests him to preach the Dharma, as is done during the Imperial Birthday or the Buddha’s birthday.

On occasions such as birthdays, the attainment of enlightenment, or the *nirvāṇa*, one should not engage in idle discourse or offer casual explanations. This is as explained in the *Jiejie Xieshu* (Explanations on Untying Knots and Offering Thanks);
its general outline concerns the protocol for descending from the seat and the etiquette of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*).

The "Small Sermon" (sōsan) and the "Five-Day Hall Sermon" (gohitsu shōdō sōsan) are matters of family precept. The Five-Day Hall Sermon serves to awaken those in training to the ultimate fact that life and death are of great importance, while also supervising the administrative affairs of the monastery;
it must be kept concise. This applies to the opening of the summer retreat, the conclusion of the summer retreat, the winter solstice, and New Year’s Eve.
Regarding the four *xiao-can* (small sermons): when the two ranks [of officials] present words of praise, one should offer thanks; at other times, it is unnecessary to lecture.

For instance, on the day of entering a new monastery, one ascends the hall and merely briefly offers thanks to the officials, the various mountain monasteries, the donors, and the members of their families; only during the night *xiao-can* does one provide a detailed account of these thanks.

When the administrative officers (*zhishi*), head monks (*tou-shou*), or special envoys arrive from afar, or when the two ranks are retained, one should prepare [the formalities] after the sermon has concluded.
Sweets and refreshments. If there are practitioners participating, they shall be assigned to the head practitioner (*sanchō*). The hall attendant shall hang the notice board.

When the evening bell tolls, the assembly gathers and stands in formation. The Abbot is invited to take his seat. The head practitioner burns incense, calls for the formal greeting, and performs nine prostrations.

The Abbot may deliver a general discourse; if there are instructions for the novices regarding their practice, these are included. Upon concluding the session, the practitioners again perform three prostrations and say, "Please take care."

The whisk was held and the formal assembly concluded during the winter season. There were four minor sermons (*sǎn*). When the Abbot requested someone to hold the whisk, [the candidate] took his seat and recited the transgressions.

On the following day, the Chief Administrator (*duìsì*), the Rector (*wéinà*), and the Attendant (*shìzhě*) delivered the whisk and the plaque to the quarters. Upon arrival, they conveyed the instructions of the Abbot; once the request to receive them was completed, the plaque was hung in public.

The boundary markers were set and the Dharma seat was arranged. In the evening, the medicinal meal was served; when the bell rang, the path was illuminated, and the Buddha-activity was concluded as the assembly descended from their seats.

The Abbot invited them to partake of soup and fruit. On the following day, tea, soup, simple rice, and the medicinal meal followed in succession. For the sake of these Zen guests, the attendants provided private hospitality.
Upon entering the Dan-guo hall, one meets the Guest Master (Ji-ke).
After the luggage has been unloaded and the feet washed, the Guest Office (Ke-si) attends to formalities. If there is a notice posted, these are suspended for the time being.

If you meet him, exchange seasonal greetings, saying: "I have long admired your reputation for the Way; now that I have had the honor of meeting you, I am filled with joy and gratitude. (If you are already acquainted, omit this. The Guest Master acknowledges this.
The guest says, "The journey here has been through many winding paths and difficult terrain; it was no easy matter to arrive. The host burns incense and serves tea.

The guest rises and says, "I am deeply grateful for your kind preparation of this tea. The host replies, "This humble tea is offered with trepidation. After the guest is escorted out, they return their formal salutation to the guest master.

Open the door first. Roll up the curtain to announce their arrival. One senior monk shall emerge from the left side to receive them and exchange formal greetings; the same procedure applies when seeing them off.
When host and guest attend to one another in this manner, there will naturally be peace and harmony.

When seeking admission to the monastery and visiting the Office of Attendants, [the official] said: "I have long admired your distinguished reputation, yet I have had no opportunity to pay my respects. Now that I am fortunate enough to have this audience, I am overcome with joy.
He bowed, rose from his seat, and addressed them, saying: "We, the newly arrived [monks], wish to pay our respects to the Master; we venture to trouble you [to grant us this audience]."
The attendant announces [the arrival]. Upon seeing the Abbot, the head of the assembly says: "We request the Venerable Master to take his seat and grant us your presence.

[The practitioners] offer incense and prostrate. The Abbot declines. They speak again: "We request the Venerable Master to accept our respect. We, the newly ordained, ought to offer incense and perform full prostrations;

we hope for your compassionate favor. If the Abbot firmly declines, they say: "Since we have received the Venerable Master’s gracious command, we shall now inquire after your well-being. (They perform a *monshin*.)

Arranging the Incense: With the left hand, take up the incense; with the right hand, tear the paper and place it inside the left sleeve. Perform two full prostrations and three partial prostrations (*zhan*). For the first *zhan*, say:

"I have long heard of your high virtue and renowned name, yet had no means to pay my respects. My arrival here today is a great fortune, that I may now behold the venerable countenance of the Venerable Master.
My humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. For the second *zhan*, say: "On this auspicious day, I respectfully wish the Abbot [well]."
"Venerable Great Master, we pray for your ten thousand blessings in health and well-being. [The assembly] performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*).

Alternatively, they may exchange greetings while standing as guests facing the host, or they may exchange greetings while seated according to the master’s position. The abbot stands before the ceremonial chair;

the participants stand in a single horizontal row, with the head participant (*chantou*) standing on the left to receive the greeting. The formalities are identical to those when seated: they sit down, drink tea, and engage in mutual inquiry and response as appropriate.
The *yi* (attendant) rises. To decline the tea, he says: "On this day, it was my duty to go to the Master’s quarters to pay my respects.

To have been granted this special preparation of tea once more is a matter for which I, your humble servant, feel profound gratitude. The Abbot may either return the courtesy immediately, or wait until the conclusion of the proceedings to do so.

The Abbot stands on the side of the host, while the *canchou* (head of the assembly) stands on the side of the guest. They enter the *danguo* (guest quarters), where they exchange greetings regarding the weather and offer their salutations, saying, "Ten thousand blessings! Just now..."

Regarding the inquiry on ritual: one should proceed to the "ten-foot" space (the master’s seat) to pay respects. Having been so graciously honored by your descent from your exalted position, our humble hearts are overcome with joy.
The abbot returns the salutation, and the assembly sees him off together. For the evening meal, we immediately prostrate ourselves, wishing you ten thousand blessings.

Today, having again been favored with your summons, our humble hearts [are filled with gratitude]... [as before]. Taking their seats, they drink tea. Once the attendant has finished burning incense and offering hot water, the abbot rises and thanks him for the tea.
[The guest] says: "I have once again received your kind hospitality" (and so forth). [The host] provides medicinal tonics and, the following morning, invites him for tea.

During the greetings, it is as before. After the ritual tea is finished, the guest thanks him and withdraws. He then requests to be granted a lodging, saying: "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift.

Having long heard of the Venerable Master’s reputation for the Way, I have come specifically to seek refuge. I beg for a single room; I hope you will graciously grant your compassionate consent. If...
The second round of recruitment is not restricted by time; it proceeds according to the immediate circumstances.

Whether through a formal inquiry or a verse, if the abbot shows even the slightest inclination, one should perform a prostration with the head touching the ground and request to be "flown" (admitted). Alternatively, one may submit a petition to the Attendant’s Office to have one's name included for dispatch.
The Hall Master then issues the official notice, saying: "By the compassionate decree of the Abbot, the Venerable [Name] is hereby admitted to the monastery on this day of this month."
The Attendant Official (Name) reports to the Hall Official (Name), the Head Seat (Name), and the Regional Official (Name): "The Precepts are here; the Head Cook has dispatched [this notice].
He says to the Abbot’s Quarters: "Inform the Hall Official and the Guest Master Attendant to request [the guests] from the *danguo*."
The [Name] Elder and others return to the hall. As there are few newly arrived monks, the Rector (Vina) bows from outside the curtain toward the master’s side to usher them in;

they perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*). They exchange greetings regarding the season and well-being (*yun-yuan*), saying, "May you have ten thousand blessings. [The Master] replies, "I am deeply honored by your reputation for the Way.

I have come here specifically to seek refuge under your guidance," and so forth. He bows to take his seat and partakes of tea. When the tea is finished, he rises and reports, "Just now, I received the compassion of the Abbot..."

The gist is as follows: Upon being assigned to a residence (guādá), each person prepares their own name and attaches it to the *dùdí* (ordination certificate). The Rector (wéinà) receives the order and hands over the *dùdí*. [The newcomer] performs one prostration.

Once the formal lecture on the monastic calendar (*shàngtáng lì*) is concluded, the *dùdí* is returned. [The newcomer] performs another prostration. The Rector escorts them back to the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*).

The Guest Master (*kètóu*) notifies the Head of the Quarters (*liǎoshǒuzuò*), or, in large monasteries where there is a Quarters Master (*liáozhǔ*), he notifies the Quarters Master. He then leads the newcomer out to perform the formalities of being assigned to a residence.

In front of the quarters, the wooden board is struck three times. The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina-zhu) bows toward the side of the master and enters the quarters, performing a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*).

He escorts [the visiting guest] out through the door. The head of the assembly (*candou*) then turns back to stand by the side of the guests and waits for the quarters. The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) comes outside the curtain and receives them, performing a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground.
They exchange greetings regarding the season (*yunyun*) and offer their salutations (*wanfu*). "I have long heard of your reputation for the Way, yet I have had no opportunity to pay my respects."

"I am fortunate to have found refuge here; for all matters henceforth, I rely upon your honorable protection. Having finished tea, he rises. The *sanchō* (head of the assembly) reports: "I have just been sent back by the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master);
it would be a blessing if you would graciously permit me to stay in the upper quarters (*jōryō*). He replies: "I accept your command.

The *sanchō* stands in a single row and performs a prostration with the head touching the floor (*chokurei*). Turning toward the side of the *shuso* (head seat), he performs one prostration. Turning toward the side of the visiting guest, he performs one prostration. The head of the quarters [performs the same].
The presiding seat-holder (zuozhanzhu) stands facing Guanyin. The head of the assembly (canchou) stands in a single file according to the following order and performs a formal greeting (wenxun).

Starting from the side of the presiding seat-holder, they perform a greeting and proceed in succession to circumambulate the Guanyin pavilion once. The head seat (shouzuo) returns to his original position and stands there, performing one greeting.

He then turns back toward the guests' side and performs a brief greeting. Alternatively, if the attendant of the quarters (chuliao zhu) performs the ritual of human affairs (renshi), it concludes at this point.
The Head Seat (Liao Shouzuo) comes forward to exchange greetings. He performs a single prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*) and, after exchanging seasonal pleasantries, says:

"I humbly wish that the Abbot of this Hall (*liaoyuan chanshi*) enjoys ten thousand blessings. [The Head Seat] then stands before [the Abbot] and says: "The head of the retreat group (*canchou*), leading the assembly, has completed the circuit of the four desks.

The Guest Master (*ketou*) then carries out the "flying" greetings to all the various quarters. Upon meeting the various Head Officers (*toushou*), each performs one prostration and exchanges seasonal pleasantries, saying: "I humbly wish that [Name] enjoys ten thousand..."

[May you] enjoy all blessings. (Narrating the departure: Whether one is an acquaintance or a close friend, once the affairs with the various officials of the quarters have been concluded, one proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to offer thanks for being granted residency.
If the Abbot receives the two-fold prostration (*liang-zhan*), one should address him with seasonal greetings, saying: "I humbly wish you ten thousand blessings.

It is by great fortune that I am now honored by your inclusion, having been permitted to follow at the end of the ranks of the dragon and elephant [sages]. [The rest of] the humble sentiments are as follows. [This applies to] the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and attendants (*shizhe*). At their respective stations...
Regarding personnel matters: there is no bowing; one immediately exchanges greetings regarding the weather and performs the standard ritual inquiries.

If it is a person of high standing (a "great guest"), the Hall Superintendent (Tangsi) shall receive them and hand over the official ordination certificate (du-jié). Once this is completed, the Guest Master (Ketu) leads them to the Sangha Hall.

The Head of the Assembly (Cantou) bows before the Sacred Monk (the image of the Buddha), burns a single stick of incense, performs three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (da-zhan san-bai), and then turns to perform a brief inquiry. He then circumambulates the hall once, starting from the seat of the Head Seat (Shouzuo), and returns to his original position.
Inquire after the health of the Venerable Sangha. Then, proceed to the attendant’s seat and sit briefly in the third position.

The *xingzhe* (attendant) informs the *weina* (ritual master). Upon reaching the head of the assembly (*candou*), lead the group in rising; exchange formal greetings with the *weina* according to the protocol of host and guest.

Return the *dujie* (ordination certificate) with one prostration. The head of the assembly turns toward the host’s side and performs another prostration. Alternatively, the *weina* may exit through either the front or rear gate.
Only the head of the assembly (the *tsan-tou*) may not be sent outside. Next, the guest master (*ke-tou*) and attendants lead him to the communal quarters (*chung-liao*).

The striking of the board for the formal greeting (*jen-shih*) is identical in ritual procedure to that for a junior resident monk (*hsiao-kua-ta*). Once he has returned to the hall, the evening medicinal meal is served in the Abbot’s quarters.
Briefly observe the usual etiquette as before. On the following day, the Abbot invites the assembly for tea;

the administrative office (Kusi) provides tea, medicine, and food, and one should immediately return the courtesy gift upon receipt, or perhaps return them all together prior to the commencement of the summer retreat. The administrative officers (Zhishi) and heads of departments (Tou-shou) also provide return gifts.

For three days, one must not go out for leisurely excursions. Attend to the serving of tea and soup. Upon returning to the quarters, the Head of the Quarters (Liao Shouzuo) offers a special bowl of hot water (tang).
The Hall Office prepares special hot water. When the four-watch bell strikes, the head officers are invited to advance and withdraw;

the Chief Seat (Śrāmaṇera) leads his colleagues to the Abbot’s quarters (Vihāra), where they perform a single prostration and announce their departure. At the time of eating congee, he issues the command.
The attendant invites [a certain person] to the abbot’s quarters for tea. The abbot personally rises to offer incense. They return to their positions and stand still.
He announces: "The former head official has retired; we now respectfully invite [a certain person] to serve as the official for [a certain] office.
The attendant invites him to perform a prostration with full touching (*chuli*) to the abbot. They turn their chairs and drink the soup. The abbot dismisses them and invites one of the senior elders.

The Head Seat (shouzuo) accompanies [the abbot] while the Monastic Administrator (janshi) parts ways; the remaining officers line up on both sides. The Attendant (shizhe) specifically burns incense for them.

The Head Seat rises to thank [the abbot] for the medicinal soup. The ritual attendant strikes the hall bell in front of the quarters, and the Abbot, together with the assembly, escorts the head officers back to their lodgings.
First, the Head Seat (Śraddhādeśaka) is sent back to his bowl-position; the Abbot bows to him. Next, he returns to the quarters for formal greetings.

The Abbot stands on the host’s side, enters the inner screen, and performs a prostration with touching of the head to the ground (chuli). He escorts him out for the handover of duties. The former Abbot stands on the host’s side while the new guest stands on the other side, and they bow once.

Furthermore, each of them bows once to the other as the new guest passes by the host. Alternatively, when a Head Seat of renowned virtue from various regions has finished ascending the seat, the Abbot [performs the same rites].

Before the Dharma seat, he prostrates together with the assembly. After the invitation, he performs the regular rites for the inspection of the quarters (*línliáo*). Alternatively, the Abbot may specially provide a medicinal broth (*tāng*) in the evening;
or the Kitchen Office (*kùsī*) distributes the medicinal broth, and he performs the rites for the morning meal (*yàoshí*). On the second day, there is tea and a simple meal from the Abbot’s quarters;
the special provisions continue, and tea, broth, and the five flavors are sent to him. East and West must thus attend to one another.

Regarding the procedure for entering and leaving, the administrative officers (zhishi) shall prepare in advance by going to the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) at the tolling of the first evening bell. They shall perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (chuli) and withdraw.
Next, the junior *weina* strikes the meal gong (*bian shichui*) until it is finished. The *jianse* leads his colleagues through the rear gate and strikes the gong.
He makes a formal announcement: “I inform the assembly: Yesterday, I was honored by the Abbot with the appointment to serve in the administrative office (kusi).

However, as I have been laboring with my mind and strength, I now request to retire and return to the hall. Having made this announcement, he first bows before the sacred monk (shengseng) at the head of the hall.

Then, turning back, he bows before the abbot, performs two prostrations with the hands opened and three prostrations with the hands closed, and finally returns to the center before the sacred monk to perform three full prostrations (dazhan sanbai). Thereafter—

Having circumambulated the hall once and exited, after the gruel meal has concluded, he orders the *xingzhe* (attendant) to call out: "I request the assembly to hang their alms bowls; I request the administrators and attendants to do the same.
He burns a single stick of incense before each saintly image, circumambulates the hall once, and without exiting the hall, bows in greeting (*wenshen*) before the Abbot.
Turning his body to the right, he stands at the edge of the assembly. The Abbot then takes the written notice from his breast pocket and hands it to him.
The attendant returns and stands beside the sacred monk’s screen. Striking the mallet once, he says: "Before the assembly, the administrative officers announce their retirement from duty.
This office must not be left vacant; having just received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, we now invite [Name] to serve as [Title] Officer.
This is respectfully announced. He strikes the mallet once more. The attendant then instructs the acolytes to invite him before the Abbot.
First, perform one prostration. Then, strike the mallet twice and announce: "The notification of the administrative officers is concluded.

The person receiving the office performs two prostrations with hands opened and three prostrations before the Abbot. Thereupon, they turn from behind the curtain, face the Sacred Monk, perform three full prostrations with hands opened, and rise.

The *vinaya-dhara* leads the procession around the hall once. Upon reaching the lower section, the attendant (*xingzhe*) calls out. The administrative officials (*zhishi*) perform prostrations with thanks.

The assembly performs three prostrations with touching of the heads (*chuli*). The assembly returns the bows. The attendant calls out again, requesting the assembly to escort the new administrative official back to the storehouse.

The new official exchanges formal greetings with the abbot, performing three prostrations with touching of the heads. They exchange pleasantries regarding the weather and so forth, hand over their duties, and withdraw. [End of] Chapter One.

When the assembly has finished their meal, the new administrative officers (xin zhixi) carry incense and visit the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to express their gratitude to the abbot; if they are taking leave, this may be waived.

They may perform a prostration with touching the ground (chuli). Subsequently, they tour the various quarters (liaos), where special refreshments and simple meals are served for them, established according to local custom.

"Please wait," [the candidate] replies. The Hall Administrator (Tangsi) then requests the Rector (Weina) to invite [the candidate], saying: "The Senior Monk (Shangzuo) [Name] is appointed as the Attendant (Shizhe) for [Name]. The Rector invites him for tea.
When the tea is finished, he rises and burns a stick of incense, reporting: "I have just received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot (Fangzhang), who requests [Name]..."

[The new] attendant [named] Chong [does so]. Having been granted the request, he rises and performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*). He then proceeds together to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). Once the *vinaya-master* (*weina*) has finished reporting to the Abbot, the attendant burns incense and performs prostrations.

He escorts the new person back to the Attendants’ Office (*shisi*). He escorts the former person back to the communal dormitory (*zhongliao*), where they exchange formal greetings (*renshi*) with the Head of the Dormitory (*liaoshouzuo*).

When the greetings are concluded, an attendant leads both the new and former members on a tour of the dormitories (*xunliao*). If one is invited to serve as the head of a branch monastery from another region...
The Horn (Jiǎo). After the reconciliation, he requests [the guest] from the Hall Attendant (*táng-sī*) or requests him directly from the Abbot’s quarters (*fāng-zhǎng*).

Afterwards, he reports the matter to the Rector (*wéi-ná*). The Abbot presides over all the ceremonial protocols. When requesting new or former head administrators (*tóu-shǒu* and *zhī-shì*), tea, soup, meals, medicinal decoctions, and refreshments are served;

for the Head Seat (*shǒu-zuò*), the attendant (*shì-zhě*) personally makes the request, while for subordinate head administrators, the attendant orders the novices (*xíng-zhě*) to make the request. At the midday meal (*zhāi*),...

The morning snack. The special soup before the end of the meditation session (*fangcan*). The ritual procedures are as previously described. Next, one proceeds to the invitation for the midday meal (*yaoshi*).

When the evening bell tolls, the Abbot visits the various quarters to serve the soup. He is received in each quarter and arranged accordingly; the attendant monks wait for the Abbot to arrive at the host’s seat in the quarters.
The attendants (*xingzhe*) arrange the soup bowls, and lamps and candles illuminate the path as they bow and invite him to sit. The chief attendant (*shizhe*) burns incense. Second.

At night, when the bell tolls, the Chief Administrator (Du-si) also patrols the quarters to serve hot water. The Chief Administrator takes his place according to the guest’s side and observes the etiquette of host and guest;
he rises personally to burn incense for the Venerable Abbot’s serving of hot water. The two classes of officials offer thanks, whereas those from the administrative office (Ku-si) do not.

When the fruits for the Venerable Abbot’s serving of hot water are brought into the hall, the Attendant burns incense (the ritual concludes here; incense is not burned again during the subsequent rounds).
**Recitation (including various types of recitation; Essential Regulations for the Hall Administrator)** 38. Recitation:

After the midday meal, the hall administrator (táng-sī xíng-zhě) reports and hangs the notice board, then informs the Abbot. Before the morning session, the great bell is struck to assemble the assembly, who stand before the hall.
The administrative officers (zhī-shì) occupy the upper section, while the Head Seat (shǒu-zuò) occupies the lower section; the rest of the assembly follows the seating diagram of the hall.

The abbot stands in meditation. He enters the hall to burn incense, followed by his attendant. Upon reaching the hall, the abbot burns incense and performs three prostrations (in some places this is omitted).
Fearing that the assembly may stand for too long, when they are about to reach the front of the hall, the ritual assistant strikes the bell.
The *vinaya-dhara* waits for the abbot to enter the hall and burn incense; meanwhile, the guest-inviting attendant requests hot water at the front of the hall and first offers a formal greeting.

When the Head Seat has finished his circuit, the administrative officers and attendants return to their positions. As the Abbot is about to exit the hall, the Rector returns to the center and stands to one side, chanting.
He must chant with a slow pace and a clear, resonant voice. On the third, thirteenth, and twenty-third days of the month, he chants:

"May the imperial wind forever fan, may the sovereign way flourish afar, may the Buddha-sun increase its brilliance, and may the Wheel of Dharma constantly turn. [He then chants] "Galan Tu... (The Earth of the Monastery).
The Earth. May the Dharma be protected and its practitioners protected. May the donors of the ten directions increase in merit and wisdom; this serves as a supreme and auspicious condition.
Contemplate the Ten Buddhas of the Pure Dharma Realm (etc.). On the eighth, eighteenth, and twenty-eighth days, one should inform the great assembly:
"Since the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered Parinirvāṇa until the fourth year of the Jǐngdìng era of the Imperial Sòng dynasty, two thousand two hundred and one years have already passed."

In the thirteenth year, [the lifespan] increases accordingly with each passing year. Yet once this day has passed, one's life is likewise diminished. Like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be?
You all should exert yourselves with diligent effort, as if your hair were on fire. Contemplate only impermanence; be careful not to be negligent.

For the sake of the monastery grounds, the protection of the Dharma and the protection of the people, and for the increase of merit and wisdom for donors from the ten directions—for these reasons, one recollects the ten Buddhas of the Pure Dharma Body.
Upon finishing the recollection, the Abbot enters first and stands in his designated place. The Head Seat chants the verse as the assembly enters the hall.
The three [monks] facing the Holy Sangha perform a greeting by bowing their heads once, then turn their bodies to perform another greeting. The Abbot receives them.

The *xuntang zhishi* (hall-inspection official) is subsequently ordered to form a patrol team for the hall inspection. They take their seats according to the diagram and consume the medicinal soup (*tang*).

When the soup is finished, the *fanzhan* bell is struck three times. The assembly performs a *wennan* (bow). The abbot exits the hall first; the *shouzuo* and the rest of the assembly each leave their seats.
If there is no soup to be consumed, the hall inspection is not required; one simply concludes with the recitation and immediately orders an attendant to call out: "Dà... (Great...).
The assembly is exempted from the hall circuit. The bell is likewise struck three times, after which the community performs a *vaṃdana* and disperses.
Prior to the summer retreat, a special tea service for newly arrived monks is prepared; the formal notice for this is posted before the communal quarters.
This morning, following the conclusion of the midday meal, the Abbot has retired to his quarters. A single serving of tea will be offered specifically for the newly arrived Head Seat.
We humbly entreat the compassion of the assembly to deign to descend together and grace this occasion; it would be most fortunate.
On this day of this month, [Name], Attendant Official, respectfully informs.

The names of those present are listed below (the signatures must be written in true calligraphy; for those with two-character names, write "respectfully prostrating at the venerable command"; for the evening medicine, the small memorial stone is hung).
The Abbot of the Hall invites the newly appointed Head Seat for the medicinal meal this evening.
On the [day] of this month, the guest attendant [Name] has received these instructions.
Form for the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera-pramukha) to Request Tea for Newly Arrived Monks Prior to the Summer Retreat.

The Head Seat Bhikṣu [Name] respectfully informs you: This morning, following the conclusion of the midday meal, we shall gather at [Name]’s location to serve one round of tea, specifically for the newly arrived Head Seat Chan Master.
We humbly entreat your compassionate presence to grace this occasion with your arrival.
On this day of this month, the Head Seat Bhikṣu [Name] submits this memorial.
Hereafter, the names of newly arrived monks shall also be listed and posted before the communal quarters; they shall be signed by the assembly.

Regarding the current practice of writing "zhī" (知) [for the recipient's name]: this is not correct according to the scriptural texts. One should write "[Name]" instead. Respectfully acknowledging your command.

The formal style for the Chief Seat of the Monastery is identical to this. If it says "formal letter" (zhuàng), then there is an envelope; for those above this rank, one performs a prostration and presents it as a special offering.
It is the same as before. Prior to the summer retreat, the Tea Kusi (Tea Office) specifically prepares for the newly arrived monks together with the Head Seat.
On one day, at the Zhao Hall, they arrange the seating positions and set up the bamboo blinds and curtains. After the morning gruel has been served, [the ceremony proceeds].
The formal petition and the ritual procedures are as previously stated. The practitioner arranges the name tablets. After the meal, the wooden board is struck.
The participants stand in their positions according to the tablets, then proceed from the four corners to bow to those seated, returning to their original places.

Once they observe that everyone has withdrawn their feet, they rise to offer incense. They then follow the order of the rows, starting from the head of the row—whether there be one or two—and proceeding to the final position.
At the [offering] station, one should inquire after [the guest's well-being], then return to the center for a brief inquiry, and finally withdraw to one’s own position. Tea is served;

when the tea service is finished, one rises and exchanges the standard greetings with the newly arrived guests. If the *Kūsi* (Storehouse Office) or *Kakushi* (Guest Office) has received them later and performs a special reception, then follow the aforementioned protocol.

After the formal greeting (*jinshang tang*) for the resolution of the knot has concluded, the attendant monk is ordered to move the incense table forward. The Chief Administrator (*dutong*) and the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) together lift the incense; sometimes the West Hall Abbot (*xitang*) does the same.
In some places, the West Hall Abbot performs this as a separate formal greeting first, performing two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations (*liangzhan sanbai*). One.

He unfolds the scroll and says: "At this time of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), when the feet are restrained, I have had the honor of serving you with the water pitcher and towel. I rely solely upon the Dharma-power of the Master to ensure that no difficulties arise.

Once again, I unfold [this] to address the season’s warmth... (and so forth). He withdraws, performs three prostrations with the forehead touching the ground, and remains as a junior disciple-attendant.

After performing prostrations, the administrative officer (zhishi) returns to the storehouse. The Head Seat (shouzuo) leads the assembly to the storehouse and performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (chuli). Next, they return to the front of the hall.

The Head Seat stands in the upper section, while the Secretary (shuji), together with the rest of the assembly, stands in the lower section. They perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground.

After the formal greetings have concluded, they take their positions according to the "Diagram for Circulating the Hall" (xuntang tu). The eminent West Hall monks (xidang) first return to their positions in the hall circuit, followed by the Head Seat.

Proceeding in succession, he leads the assembly on a circuit of the hall. Having completed one round, they return to the hall and take their places. The *xingzhe* (attendant) cries out: "The Head Seat prostrates in thanks;

the assembly bows three times" (chanting: "The assembly performs the general salutation"). The administrative officers (*zhishi*) enter the hall, face the Sacred Monk, and perform three full prostrations with the robes spread wide.

They then complete a circuit of the hall and return to stand at the head of the central row. The *xingzhe* cries out: "The administrative officers prostrate in thanks; the great assembly bows three times. The administrative officers...

The procedure begins: The bell in front of the hall is struck to signal the gathering. The Abbot enters the hall, offers incense, and performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).

He then circumambulates the hall once. The junior monks exit through the rear door to avoid him. Once the Abbot has returned to his position in the hall and stands still, the attendant calls out, "Venerable!
The Abbot then exchanges greetings with the assembly with three prostrations. Next, the attendant burns incense and serves tea.
For the Great Special Tea (the format for the notice is provided previously; the attendant prepares the ritual and invites the Head Seat).

At the time of the midday meal, when the long board gong sounds, the attendant enters the hall and burns incense. He performs three full prostrations with his mat spread out (*dazhan sanbai*), circumambulates the hall once, and performs one prostration before the hall.
First he goes to the lower section, then the upper section, and finally returns to the center. He bows in greeting and withdraws. If it is the Abbot or the Head Seat...

When requesting tea while seated and performing the ritual, first the former abbot (senzo) and the monks [are served]; then, turning back toward the abbot, one bows in greeting before him. Next, the procession through the hall is the same as before.
Prior to the midday meal, the embroidered coverings are arranged and the name-boards (shōhaku) are set out; these are invited into the hall, accompanied by the administrative officers (chiji).

The head seat (shuso) prepares his position facing the abbot, with the chief administrator (toso) in the same row. At the front entrance, the subordinate administrators separate from the group. Behind...
At the gate, the hand-drum sounds. The attendants wait before the hall for the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to take his place. They request the Head Seat to rise and request the one below him to rise.
The Abbot escorts the Head Seat to the assigned seat. Upon returning outside the hall, the bell is struck to receive the Abbot as he takes his seat.

Next, burn incense before the Buddha in the inner, outer, upper, and lower sections. Return to your original position and perform a greeting. Next, perform a greeting before the Head Seat (Shouzuo). Return to the front of the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ).

Pass through the hall on patrol and, upon reaching the interior of the gate, stand at the position of the Administrative Head (Wudusi). Next, [burn incense] in the upper and lower sections outside the hall.

Return and stand before the Standing Buddha, awaiting the serving of tea. When it is nearly time, again perform a greeting before the Head Seat to offer encouragement for the tea, and return to the Holy Monk.
Before the Sangha, perform three full prostrations with the robes spread out. Circumambulate the hall as before. Next, collect the cups from the Abbot’s quarters and the Head Seat.

The Head Seat rises and proceeds to the front of the Abbot’s quarters, performs two spreads and three prostrations, and says once: "I humbly receive your compassionate favor in granting me this special prior serving" (and so forth).

He then spreads his robes again and says: "The weather is warm. Stepping back, he performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground. He exits through the front gate from behind the screen curtains, while the Abbot sees him off.
[The Abbot] exits. He returns to his seat in the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters) and holds up the cup. The attendant burns a single stick of "accompanying incense" (*xiangban xiang*).

Then, the drum is struck three times. The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) goes to the *fangzhang* to offer thanks; this may also take place in the Dharma Hall. If it is the evening of the summer retreat (*jie xia*), the ritual for the special medicinal soup (*tetang li*) follows the same procedure as sitting for the medicinal food (*yaoshi*).
The Prior (*jian si*) observes the Head Seat’s thanksgiving for the soup, and once [the Head Seat] reaches his own position and sits down, he then follows suit.
Go forward to the front to perform a greeting (*wensun*). Turn behind the screen and return to the center; perform a greeting and burn incense.

Having finished burning the incense, first perform a greeting before the current abbot, then before the Head Seat (*shouzuo*), and next before the Upper Seat (*shangbu*). This is the regular etiquette for the hall. The attendant (*xingzhe*) then calls out the invitation.

The assembly lowers their bowls for the medicinal food (yàoshí). When the medicinal food is finished, the drum is struck three times and they exit the hall. They perform a collective prostration in front of the hall;
the *jiànsì* specifically leads the prostration for the *shouzuo*, and the *shouzuo* specifically leads it for the *zàngzhǔ* (as for the tea ceremony, see above).

When the long board is sounded, incense is burned and the circuit of the hall is performed with prostrations. Furthermore, regarding the bowing upon sitting after the meal and the burning of incense to perform the rites, these are not recorded again here.
This is merely the Tea Service. Perform three full prostrations. First, inquire after the head seat (shouzuo); then, the abbot inquires after you.
Circumambulate the hall once starting from the head of the platform. As the tea is about to be collected, the abbot and the head seat each receive two portions of the cups.

The administrative officials (zhishi) lead their colleagues before the abbot and perform two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations to express thanks for the tea. They escort the abbot out first.

In front of the Hall. Afterwards, escort the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to the front of the Hall and perform a prostration by touching the ground once. The same procedure applies when the Head Seat specifically serves as the Librarian (Zangzhu).
The format for the Tea Notice (Teabang): (The procedure for the Soup [Tang] is the same; invite the tea early by taking incense to the Abbot’s Quarters.)

The administrative office (Kusi) has now, following the midday meal this morning, prepared a single serving of tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly, as a modest mark of ceremony for [the commencement of the retreat until the festival, and the conclusion of the retreat at the end of the year]. We humbly hope that all will graciously deign to join us in this auspicious occasion; it would be most fortunate.
On this day of this month, the *kusi* bhikṣu [Name] respectfully requests. Format for the Request Form for Tea by the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*):
The bhikṣu [Name], Head Seat, having retired from the midday meal this morning, shall serve one round of tea in the Cloud Hall (*yundáng*) specifically for the Librarian (*zhīzàng*).
This document respectfully records the ceremonial protocols for the commencement of the retreat (*jie-zhi*) until its conclusion (*jie-zhi*), as well as the New Year offerings.

We hereby invite the Abbot of the Rear Hall, the Scribe, the Meditation Master, and the entire assembly, as well as all the administrative officers (*zhishi*), to graciously descend and attend. Respectfully submitted.
On this day of this month, the Head Seat Bhikṣu [Name] submits this formal petition.
Respectfully sealed by the Bhikṣu [Name], who was the first invited to serve as Head Seat.
Notice for the Medicinal Confections (to be posted below the lower section of the hall entrance):
The administrative office (Kusi) will tonight provide one set of medicinal confections in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly.

This is intended as a modest mark of ceremony [for the commencement of the retreat until the festival, or for the conclusion of the retreat at the end of the year]. We humbly hope that all the venerable ones will deign to descend and grace us with their presence. It would be most fortunate.
On this day of this month, the monastery administrator (kusi) bhikṣu [Name] respectfully requests.
If the Abbot encounters the end of the winter retreat (jie-jie dong-nian), he should first write a small notice and affix it beneath the notice for the medicinal broth (tang-bang),
thereby exempting [the guest] from the formal greetings of the following morning.

Tomorrow morning, the retreat (jiezhi) will commence. It is appropriate that the two classes of elders, Dharma relatives, junior disciples, and local acquaintances should, upon the conclusion of the formal lecture, proceed directly to the Dharma Hall to exchange general greetings;
there is no need for individual visits. This is specially submitted for your information, and we earnestly hope you will take this to heart.
Regarding the protocol for consultation and reception:

when visiting other mountains, one should proceed as if a great venerable elder (dazunsu) were arriving at a temple; one should immediately arrange the meeting according to the etiquette of host and guest, with each person offering incense and performing three prostrations.
Next, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*), the heads of the assembly (*sthavira*), and the general community shall act as a single unit to perform the task of offering incense.

They shall prostrate themselves to test whether [the guest] will accept the offering or not. Next, the attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) shall offer incense and prostrate; the ritual assistant (*karmika*) shall call for the invitation. The administrative officers and heads of the assembly shall accompany [the guest] to consume the medicinal broth (*yūṣa*);
however, this is merely a formal courtesy using empty cups. Alternatively, if it is a dharma-relative, a junior disciple, or an attendant who offers incense and prostrates, next—

The temple’s head attendant (*sanda*) leads the assembly to carry incense and perform prostrations. The accompanying attendants and laborers brought along for the visit follow behind to perform their prostrations.

Once the host has finished drinking the medicinal broth (*tō*), the administrative officers (*chiji*) and heads of departments (*shushu*) escort the guests to their assigned quarters. The guest and host prepare incense and gifts;
