there are no formal prostrations, and they exchange pleasantries regarding the weather and the season (as detailed). Next, the administrative officers, heads of departments, attendants (*shijō*), and Dharma relatives [perform the same].

The Master and his acquaintances exchange greetings according to their seniority. The Abbot, accompanied by the attendant, leads them on a tour of the quarters. That evening, a special soup service is held specifically for this occasion.
The invitation states: "This evening, the Head Monk will serve soup in the Meditation Hall; we hope you will grant us your presence. There is no formal exchange regarding the weather.

The two classes of officers accompany one another to partake of the soup. Upon the sounding of the drum, they enter to pay their respects to the Head Monk. Prior to this, [the guest] has already visited the quarters.

Retreat: three beats on the drum. Accompanied by *yàoshí* (medicinal stone/food), it is requested by the person [in charge]. When the evening bell tolls, accompanied by hot water and fruit, there follows the special meal (*tèwéifàn*), which is requested by the *kùsī* (storehouse office).
Together with the attendant, they go to the place where the guest is staying, light incense together, and perform one prostration (there are cases where no prostration is made).
The *jiānsì* (abbot’s assistant) requests the meal; the attendant then makes the formal invitation. After the abbot’s midday meal concludes, tea is specially served. Respectfully.

I pray for your compassion. Please grant your permission to accompany you. You may invite [the guest] to sit at ease according to your wish; or, if they are a Dharma relative or a junior disciple, they may perform prostrations as is customary.

As for the abbots of various mountains, they shall simply exchange formal greetings. If it is a member of one’s own Dharma lineage who meets them, the inferior should request the superior to take the seat of honor.

Burn incense and perform two prostrations. If a superior meets an inferior, although the host occupies the position of host, they shall set up a temple seat in the center and wait for the guest to take their place.
They shall invite a senior elder to accompany them, either for tea or to perform prostrations specifically for the sake of the person.

This is practiced by human beings. When scholars of renown from various regions arrive at the mountain monastery, they submit a formal petition requesting that [the abbot] ascend the seat to inspire and uplift the junior students. The format for such a petition is as follows:
[The Petition Form]

The undersigned, [Name], of the [Surname] clan, residing at [Name of Abbot’s Office] (or Name of Administrative Head’s Office), respectfully submits this humble petition. We pray that you will uphold the fundamental tenets and enlighten future students.
We humbly beseech your compassionate grace to deign to accept us under your guidance. This is respectfully submitted.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], [Name of Person], holding the rank of [Title], submits this memorial. Regarding the regulations for the bells and drums:

the great bell is struck one hundred and eight times during both the morning and evening services. This applies to the recitations performed at the commencement and conclusion of the ritual, as well as when receiving high-ranking officials and the newly appointed abbot.

One strike for passing through the hall; seven strikes of the bell before the hall (seven strikes to retire from the hall, three strikes for the end of the *ch'an* session); one strike each for assembling the assembly at the front of the hall, the main shrine, and other locations;

three strikes of the drum for ascending the hall; one strike for entering the hall to announce the meal; three strikes for taking leave of the assembly; two strikes for both meals (morning and evening);

five strikes for the general discourse (*pusō*) and the incense offering (*gok-hyang*); two strikes for the small discourse (*sān-p'aram*) and the ritual of holding the broom; and when a patron arrives, the two ranks of officials strike the drum at the entrance.
Five strikes of the bell below. One round of drums to escort the assembly. Three rounds of the bathing drum to establish the sequence.
A special messenger is sent to invite the Abbot;

once the incumbent has arrived at that location, he first visits the Guest Master, then the administrative officers, and after settling into his quarters, he prepares the formal letter of introduction.

The notice is posted above the main hall of the dormitory. The abbot comes out to exchange greetings, presents his petition for consultation, and burns incense before the notice, performing three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).
The guest master leads the various quarters to exchange greetings. If the invited head officers, administrative officials, or elders enter the gate, the same procedure is followed.

First, the Guest Master (Kechi) is informed. The Guest Master leads him to an audience with the Abbot (Fangzhang), who then escorts him to his quarters. Next, he proceeds to the Administrative Office (Kusi) to conduct formal greetings with the various departments.
He then returns with the Attendant (Shizhe) to the Abbot’s quarters to report: "The Abbot of [Name] Monastery has now invited [Name] to serve as the Abbot. This is concluded immediately.
The Head Officers (Tou-shou) then go together to the [invited monk's] quarters to extend the invitation. They arrange the formal documents (shu-tie) in the Dharma Hall, and the Host takes his place.

First, the presiding master leads the assembly to the hall and descends from his seat. Next, the new host presents the ceremonial notice (tiē) and the formal discourse (fǎyǔ). The rector (weínná) proclaims the memorial (shū), which is then handed to the secretary (shūjì) to read.

If there are further instructions from the head officers (tóushǒu), they shall be proclaimed and read as well. If the recipient has not yet left the household life (wèichūshìrén), the Dharma robe (fǎyī) is presented;

if there is a formal discourse, the new person receives the robe and puts it on. Afterwards, he is directed to the Dharma seat (fǎzuò); having ascended and descended from the seat, he exchanges greetings with the host.

The administrative head (zhishi tóushou) shall inform the assembly of the personnel matters. Subsequently, the Abbot and the Head Seat, together with the assembly, shall escort [the guest] to his quarters.

The Guest Prefect shall lead him on a tour of the monastic cells. Afterwards, a vegetarian meal in accordance with the invitation shall be prepared, followed by a special tea service for the Mountain Gate. On the day of departure, [the same protocol shall be observed].
A seat and canopy are set up at the three gates, and a special *táng-lǐ* (tea ceremony) is performed. This is the same as the special tea and soup ceremony for various guests.
The exclusive messenger’s meal is arranged within the Sangha Hall; the new host sits facing the previous host, just as in the current practice. No other [seating] is required.
Arranging the Seats: The special envoy shall personally go to pay respects and extend the invitation.

When the attendant of the quarters announces the time for the meal, the special envoy shall wait in the hall for the host and the newly ordained person to enter (bowing as they take their seats, burning incense). First, he shall inquire after the host; next, he shall inquire before the newly ordained person;
thereafter, he shall inquire throughout the upper and lower sections of the hall and outside the hall. He shall re-enter the hall to inquire once more, and then depart.
They eat their meal outside the hall. Next, they burn incense and present the under-tablets (chèn): first the incumbent abbot, then the new appointee, and finally the assembly of monks.
Once the tablets have been presented, they perform a bow of inquiry (wènxùn). Tea is served; when the tea pitcher is brought out, the cups for the abbot and the new appointee are collected first.

The special messenger proceeds directly to the rear gate and stands before the new appointee, performing two prostrations with opened sitting cloths (liǎnzhǎn) and three full prostrations (sānbài), then escorts him out through the rear gate. Next, he goes before the abbot and likewise...
The two [the host and the guest] perform the full prostrations (*dazhan*) together; they rise at the same time. The special messenger escorts them out through the front gate.
At some locations, the new person is first escorted out through the front gate, followed by the abbot of the monastery being escorted out of the hall.

Once the host has exited and performed the inquiry (*wenxun*), they re-enter the hall, burn one stick of "accompanying incense" (*xiangban xiang*), perform three full prostrations, and circumambulate the hall once. Outside the hall, they turn back together and return to the center of the hall.

[The guest] says, "Yang" (a polite salutation). After a single inquiry after his health, the cups are collected. The drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from the hall. Next, they go to the Abbot’s quarters and the administrative office (Kusi) to offer thanks.
If the special envoy is excused, medicinal food (yao-shi) is prepared that evening. For the host and the new arrivals, when the evening bell tolls, there is hot water and fruit.
They then invite the administrators and head officers to accompany them.

When the new abbot enters his residence, he must first ascertain where he will be stationed. Once the introductory letter has been delivered, the senior monks (*kiju*), the two classes of officials (*ryangban*), and the assembly should collectively go to offer their greetings.
Unless the newcomer has received a formal notice (*pitt’o*) exempting him from this, the administrative officers (*jiji*) should inquire as to the date of his entry.

The Kusi (Treasury Office) notifies the Tangsi (Hall Office) to hang the announcement board. At the appointed time, the ritual implements are sounded, and the assembly exits through the three gates in formation to receive the newcomer.

This refers to the ritual performed at the Buddha Hall at the three gates; only then do they return to the hall. The newcomer performs three prostrations facing the Sacred Monk (the image of the Buddha).

The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) inquires after [the master’s] well-being and leads him on a circuit of the hall once. He then requests [the master] to return to his bowl-seat, where they perform one prostration and exit the hall.

They proceed to the Hall of the Local Deity (*tiandi*) and the Patriarchs’ Hall; there is a formal discourse (*fayu*). Next, they go to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*), where [the master] takes his seat and burns a single stick of incense. The attendant (*shizhe*) inquires after his well-being.
The Master’s Buddhist Rituals:

The Head Monastery Official (Dusi) presents the official seal and the prepared document. It is placed upon the sedan chair. The Master examines the seal; the attendant monk (Haengja) breaks the seal and presents it to the Master.
A document recording the date and signature shall be prepared; the attendant shall have the abbot affix his seal and receive that sealed document.
The robes and bowl are then entrusted [to the recipient], and the attendant shall collect them within three days. The Hall Office shall present the ordination certificate (dùdié).
Formal Memorial:
The monks of the temple’s treasury office (named so-and-so), etc., submit one seal of the monastery’s permanent property register to the newly appointed Abbot, Great Monk.
We humbly await your compassionate instructions. Respectfully submitted.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], the monk of the treasury office submits this formal petition.

The administrative officers withdraw from their seats and stand in full assembly. They burn incense, inquire after his well-being, perform two prostrations with hands extended, and three full prostrations, addressing him as follows:

"We have once again received the honor of the Venerable Master presiding over the Dharma seat; our humble feelings are such that... He replies: "I am personally ashamed of my own incompetence and clumsiness... The Head Seat [performs the same].

The assembly offers congratulations with grass mats. The practitioner issues a formal invitation. The two classes of elders present hot water in the dormitory. After the hot water is finished, the Abbot takes a short rest and partakes of refreshments.
The Chief Administrator (Dusi) carries incense and a formal letter to invite him for a meal.
Formal Memorial.

The monks of the temple’s storehouse office (Skt. *kośādhyakṣa*), [Name] and others, respectfully submit this memorial. This day at the hour of the horse (*māgha*), we shall prepare a meal in the Cloud Hall (*megha-maṇḍapa*).
We humbly entreat your venerable compassion to deign to grace us with your presence. Respectfully submitted.
The formal petition for the new appointment of the Abbot, Great Monk [Name], etc., is respectfully sealed.

The various quarters shall hang the notification boards in advance. After a short while, the attendant announces the ascent to the hall. Upon reaching the Dharma seat, the special envoy burns incense and performs the rites.
The master presents the incense tablet and extracts the Dharma words, which are then handed to the Rector (Vina) to read. Next, he presents the memorial and extracts the Dharma words.

The head official’s provisions are presented. Next, the reading is completed. Then, the instructions for ascending the Dharma seat are given. He ascends the Dharma seat; the attendant ascends with him.

Having offered incense to pray for the Emperor, he prays for the Emperor. Having finished praying for the Emperor, he offers the incense for the officials. [Name] takes the incense of the Dharma heir from his bosom and takes his seat.

The attendant follows the usual procedure. When the Master ascends the hall, the assembly files out and the two ranks take their positions. The Master solicits a topic for dialogue and engages in question-and-answer.

He presents the outline of the discourse and offers thanks. Regarding the *sō* (petition) and *sho* (certificate) for the Dharma seat, the special envoy has already instructed the attendants to prepare incense at the eastern side of the Dharma Hall early on, so that they may welcome the host upon arrival.
Once there, the envoy performs the rites, burns incense, prostrates three times with full prostration (*chūrei*), and presents the certificate.

Commentary: Afterward, before the Dharma seat, the "Nianchu" (the item for recitation) concerning the exposition of Chan is brought forward and read aloud. If there are exemptions, they are brought forward.

When the Master ascends and descends from the seat, there are ceremonies of congratulation and courtesy. In some places, the attendant first calls out for the greetings of the various mountain monasteries;

next, the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and heads (*tou-shou*) of the monastery, along with the West Hall monks (*xitang*), ascend together to offer incense—either performing two prostrations with the robes spread open followed by one prostration with the robes folded—or, if exempted, they perform a single prostration.
The ritual for the Great Assembly is likewise. Next, the Dharma-relatives, junior masters, and practitioners follow behind, taking turns offering incense.

Once the prostrations and formal greetings are completed, they tour the various quarters (*liao*). All the residents of the quarters come out to escort and welcome them, though this does not apply to the Great Assembly.

Having finished the tour of the quarters, the Chief Administrator (*dutusi*) carries incense and visits the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to request tea. In some places, there is a large banner for the tea service made of silk.
If [the person] is absent, one shall submit a formal petition. The format for the petition is as follows:

The bhikṣus (Name) et al. of this monastery, respectfully address [the name] of [Place]. Having retired from the midday meal this very day, we request that you specially attend to the rite in the Cloud Hall.
Tea. We hereby extend our formal greetings of congratulation. We humbly entreat your venerable compassion to deign to grace us with your presence. Respectfully submitted.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], the bhikṣus [Name] et al. submit this memorial.
After the tea has concluded, the Chief Administrator (Dusi) leads his colleagues in offering thanks, performing the prostrations as previously described.

If there is a special tea service (teatō), the Head Officers (Toshu) are invited to accompany the assembly; the Administrative Officers (Chiji) perform the rites, carrying the identification tablets (shōhapa).

The assembly stands before the Sangha Hall, the hall-front bell is struck, and the Abbot is ushered into the hall. He returns to his seat and bows; then, moving behind the curtain, he performs the rites for the special guests.
The ritual is the same as previously described and is not recorded again here. When it is time for tea, first collect one portion of the host’s cups;

the Chief Administrator (Dusi) and his attendants perform two prostrations with hands extended in thanks and escort them out. They then return to the hall, burn a single incense stick as a companion offering, strike the drum three times, and withdraw from the hall.
Regarding the rituals and regulations after entering the monastery, the supervision of the monastic property (changzhu) shall be carried out by the Host.

When a letter from a venerable elder of various quarters arrives, delivered by a special messenger to the temple, the messenger first sees the guest prefect (*kṣāṇavāra*), then proceeds to the attendants' office (*shìsī*), and is escorted to have an audience with the abbot.

After the customary tea ceremony is concluded, he rises, burns incense, and presents the letter along with any final instructions or items left behind. The abbot then orders an attendant to invite [the sender’s representative].
Two cups of tea are served. The messenger announces that [Name] has passed away. After the letter is opened and read, hot water is poured, and the guest is escorted to their quarters.

Next, the monks are circulated through the various offices (*liao*). The Abbot personally hands the memorial text (*jìwén*) to the Secretary (*shūjì*). The administrative office (*kùsī*) is notified to prepare the sacrificial food.

On the following day, seats are arranged in the western section of the Dharma Hall (*fǎtáng*). After the morning gruel is finished, the Abbot ascends the seat. He stands briefly before the seat; the special envoy steps forward and burns incense.
Incense is offered. The testamentary letter is presented. The abbot receives the letter, incenses it, and orders the attendant to hand it to the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to read aloud.
Afterwards, he ascends the seat to preach the Dharma. Upon finishing the sermon, he descends from the seat, burns incense, and offers three or two wails of lamentation;

otherwise, as is customary, there is no wailing. Tea and soup are served, and food is offered. The *vinaya-dhara* bows in greeting, steps out of the assembly to burn incense, and the abbot offers incense, followed by the two [disciples].
The Abbot offers incense. Having finished offering the incense, the Rector (Vina) proclaims the memorial text, recites the sutra, and performs the dedication of merit.

Depending on the gravity of the occasion—whether for a dharma relative, an old friend, or a junior disciple—one should offer words of consolation and prepare a reception, with the specific offerings provided by the special envoy varying according to the number of people present.

When the incumbent abbot is about to pass away, one should first request the administrative officers (*zhishi*) and heads of departments (*tou-shou*) to prepare a clear inventory of assets and write a verse of farewell (*ge*).

One should then entrust the various matters of the treasury office and the affairs of the community to them as a final instruction. Furthermore, one should have letters sent to the various monasteries and arrange for these documents to be placed to the west of the Dharma Hall in advance.
Having purified the hair and bathed, he puts on his robes and sits cross-legged. He enters the shrine-casket (*kaṅkāra*). He requests a senior elder (*sthavira*) to move the casket;

once the casket has been moved into its fixed position, the bell is struck and the assembly is gathered. Sūtras are chanted. The casket is placed in the center of the western side. The true likeness (*pratibimba*) is hung upon the Dharma seat (where there is ritual activity). Offerings are arranged in the center.
On the eastern side, one arranges the bed, curtains, bedding, clothing rack, hand-towel, Dharma robe, and incense table.

[The deceased] then dispatched a final letter and departed. The various mountain monasteries requested the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of their own temple to serve as the presiding mourner (*śavapati*), or they may invite someone from outside;

the assembly shall receive them. Alternatively, for the funeral inscription of the mountain gate, one should separately invite a secretary for the mourning office (*śavakarmādhikārin-lekhaka*) and a person in charge of the finances (*dhanādhyakṣa*).
He shall preside over subsequent affairs. The rituals for recitation and other matters are fully detailed in the *Tangsi Xūzhī* (The Tang Office’s Essential Knowledge).
Format for the Notification of Death:

Bhikṣu [Name], Director of Funerals at [Name] Temple. To the Right: [Name] respectfully informs you. It is with great sorrow that we announce that on the [Day] of this month, the Abbot of our mountain gate...
The Upādhyāya has suddenly returned to the truth. I respectfully submit this notification of his passing. Respectfully stated.
On the [day], [month], and [year], by the monk [Name] of the funeral office.
Sealable. This letter is respectfully submitted by the bhikṣu [Name], sealed with due care. Regarding this letter left behind, I am of no merit to this mountain;
I have merely relied upon the radiance of my neighbor’s wall. Reflecting on myself, how could I be worthy? Having realized that worldly conditions are but illusory dreams.

We were unable to meet in person for our parting; our hearts are filled with longing as we hasten toward you. We pray that on the day of the Buddha’s appearance, you will brandish the halberd [of wisdom], so that the wind of our school may be further strengthened.
(This does not apply to those who are merely human.)
The Last Letter of Master Jishi Ying, Transmitted to Upadhyaya Zai, Regarding the Waiver of Subsidies (Gutian Lingfo):

I have briefly responded to a minor karmic affinity, coming to rely upon the protection of your shade. Suddenly, I was startled by a great illusion, departing before I could gaze upon the dew on the scallions [at your funeral].

Reflecting upon my tenure as abbot at three monasteries throughout my life, I have not taken even the slightest thing belonging to the permanent endowment. My robes and bowl are meager, and my ritual implements are sparse.

I pray that you will grant me relief by providing for these necessities, thereby manifesting your compassionate and benevolent governance. A man of wisdom preserves himself; do not allow resentment to be cast upon you, which might bring harm to your person.
The retribution of karma is not in vain; I further hope that while serving in office, you will plant the seeds of merit. These are my final requests as I approach death.
There is no further occasion for a formal parting; I shall increasingly distance myself from the light of your presence. I humbly entreat you to cherish yourself.
(During the Jianding era, the official Zhang Lan received a donation of his stipend to assist with that undertaking; [he] requested the support of Mr. Dui and others.)

The *vina* (chant leader) must know how to respond with adaptability according to the occasion. His eulogies for the Buddha and his formal expositions are fully recorded in the *qinggui* (rules of purity), as are the details of his duties.

He presides over the rear section of the Sangha Hall, the communal quarters, the administrative office, the purification hall, the Longevity Hall, and the stupa grounds. He also oversees the abbot’s movements within the public precincts.

Congratulations. Wait until you have returned and hung your nameplate before notifying the assembly to receive you. If you are exempted from this, simply go to the Abbot’s quarters to pay your respects.

Regarding matters such as registering for residency, requesting leave, and the affairs of deceased monks, these must all be handled with meticulous care; do not allow them to become subjects of external gossip. Harmonize those above and below, and act in a way that earns the affection and respect of others;
this is what is called "pleasing the assembly."
Regarding the Recitation for the Sacred Festival at the Buddha Hall:

The imperial wind fans forever, and the sovereign way flourishes afar. At this time when the stars coil like sleeves and lightning flashes, and as the dawn of the birth month arrives, we respectfully assemble the pure assembly and humbly proceed to the precious sanctuary.
We chant the great names of all Buddhas to offer our prayers for the Emperor’s longevity.
By the wise calculations of men, we contemplate purity. Through the great merit of the recitations above, we pray for the boundless longevity of His Majesty the Emperor.
O Vajra Amitāyus Buddha and all the honored ones!
Stepping out of the assembly to offer incense (the administrative office [kūsī] has previously prepared the incense).
The *vinaya-dhara* first stands before the burner on the eastern side and bows. The abbot offers the incense while the attendant (*shìzhě*) holds the casket. Next, the two ranks of officials advance.

For the ceremonies commemorating the Buddha’s birthday, his attainment of enlightenment, and his parinirvāṇa, as well as for the prayers for the Emperor, they do not turn their bodies to bow. Having finished offering the incense, the ritual assistant (*xingzhě*)...
Prostrations with the *he-zhan* [chant]. At the site where the local deity has already descended, there is the ritual of turning the body to invite the incense.

For the opening and concluding ceremonies: Bathing the Buddha (the eighth day of the fourth month), Attaining Enlightenment (the eighth day of the twelfth month), and Parinirvāṇa (the fifteenth day of the second month).
On the first evening, inform the assembly. At dawn, prepare the formal regalia. The following morning, ascend the hall, descend from the Great Hall, and serve tea and soup.

The abbot steps out of the ranks to offer incense, pays homage to the Buddhas (modifying the titles as appropriate), and proclaims the memorial. The guest master passes the hand-incense burner; the abbot kneels to receive it, while the attendant kneels to present the incense.
Next, the sutra is recited, followed by the dedication of merit and the distribution of offerings. Then, the verse for the Buddha-Bath is chanted: "I now bathe all the Tathāgatas."
A mass of merit adorned with pure wisdom, causing sentient beings of the five turbidities to leave behind defilement and together realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body.
(At the Śūraṅgama Assembly, do not leave the assembly; offer incense.)

On this occasion of the Summer Retreat recitation, as the fragrant winds fan the wilds and the Lord of Fire presides over the quarter, we mark the time when the Buddha, King of Awakening, established the retreat regulations; it is the day when the Śākya clan protects all living beings.

We have personally gathered the great assembly and solemnly proceeded to the sacred shrine to chant and uphold the vast and majestic names of the myriad virtues, dedicating the merit toward [enlightenment].

The true lords of this hall desire to pray for their protection so that they may successfully attain peaceful dwelling. We respectfully rely upon the assembly to recite the names of the Ten Buddhas (*etc.*).
The merit from the foregoing recitations is offered as a dedication to the local deities of this mountain (*etc.*), the guardian deity of the monastery, and the true lords of this hall.
True Sovereign. We humbly pray that Your divine power may provide harmonious assistance, causing the meritorious deeds that benefit [all beings] to shine forth;
may the Garden of Dharma flourish and prosper, forever bestowing impartial blessings. Again we reflect upon [the ten directions and three periods of time, etc.].

The summer retreat has ended as the golden wind fans the wilds, and the White Emperor presides over the quarter. This is the moment when the Buddha, the King of Awakening, releases the retreat regulations; it is the day when the dharma-year reaches its full cycle.
Having spent the ninety days without difficulty and with the entire assembly in peace, we chant the great names of the Buddhas to offer our reverent gratitude to all those gathered in this hall.
True Sovereign. We humbly pray (as before).

As the season arrives during a year of adversity, the time of the festival coincides with the recording of the clouds; it is the beginning of the return of the first yang, when all things begin to sprout and flourish.
At its commencement (and so forth).
On the eve of the year, the Eastern Sovereign spreads his edict; the Big Dipper turns its handle. When the seventy-two seasonal signs have completed their cycle, it is then the thirty-sixth [day].

When the ten-day period of recitation concludes, whenever the bi-monthly (3rd and 8th) chanting is held, the assembly shall take their positions according to the diagram for chanting. They wait until the abbot enters the hall, burns incense, and emerges;
thereafter, they chant the names of the Ten Buddhas and perform the subtle ritual procedures. These details are clearly explained in the section on the bi-monthly chanting.
Do not raise [the gong] again. It shall be as during the *xiaocan* (informal evening discourse) that same night;
do not strike the *fangcan* (end-of-discourse) bell.

For the annual memorial service (*nianjungi*), have an attendant purchase paper in advance and write out the formal petition (*zhuangshi*). Post three copies of this petition at the lower section in front of the Hall; one copy must be written.
Province. One copy for the County. One copy for the Hall Office. Local precedents are established according to the region.
I, the monk (Name) of (Name) Temple, have now been requested by the local government authorities to provide the official register of monks for the year (Year).
It is necessary to submit this report. To the right: I am a native of (Name) County in (Name) Province. My secular surname is (Name), and I belong to the household of (Name). Currently...

At what age [did you enter the order]? You purchased [the certificate] under [Name] No. [Number] in the year [Year]. You received the *du’die* (ordination certificate) for the Way, taking [Name] of [Temple] as your preceptor.
On the [Day] of the [Month] of the year [Year], coinciding with the auspicious festival of [Name of Ruler/Saint], you opened the altar and received the precepts.

You requested the Six Recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and obtained the complete ordination certificate (*śīla-patra*). The official records of the year [Year] are kept at [Location] for submission. The items submitted are listed above; all have been presented.
Truly so. Respectfully submitted.
On the [day] of the [month] year [year], the monk [name], styled [style name], presents this memorial.
For the anniversary of the Patriarch’s passing (the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing is the fifth day of the tenth month; see *Chuan Deng Lu*).
The Hall Attendant prepares the formal petition and first reports it to the Abbot. The Head Seat then arranges offerings such as incense and flowers.

Either at the tolling of the evening bell, they chant and recite sutras; or before the midday meal, if there is no chanting, they simply step out of the assembly to burn incense, recite the scripture, and offer incense without turning their bodies back.
Reciting with deep and profound compassion and vows: the Great Way is difficult to name, yet by your grace we have been moistened by its lingering waves, bringing glory to our descendants.
Now that the anniversary of his True and Constant nature has arrived, we respectfully present these rites of remembrance; we look up to the pure assembly to recite the names of the Ten Buddhas.
[Recite the invocation: "Cloud... [Then] perform the dedication of merit as is customary.

The foregoing recitation serves as a requital for the scripture. We humbly dedicate this for the sake of the founding patriarch (Name), to repay his compassionate protection. Recite the ten directions [mantra] once more.
On the following day, chant the scripture and perform the dedication. We humbly pray that it may benefit all living beings.

When a sick monk recites these words, one must consider the layman of Vaiśālī, who still recounted the circumstances of his inquiry after illness; and the Patriarch of Niu Mountain, who yet endured the consequences of a wind ailment.
On this day, there is a certain sick monk who has unexpectedly been afflicted by a slight malady, which has consequently become chronic and for which he has repeatedly taken medicine.

Yet, as the illness has not yet subsided, I contemplate that this illusory body is not substantial. I respectfully assemble the pure assembly in harmony to recite, with one voice, the great names of the Buddhas, thereby sweeping away the demonic afflictions so they may depart.
I look up to the venerable assembly to recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* (The Pure Dharma Body).

The foregoing recitation is offered on behalf of the sick monk [Name], praying for his peace and security. We humbly beseech that if his remaining conditions are not yet severed, he may soon attain health and tranquility;
if his allotted lifespan is difficult to evade, may he be swiftly reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).

Furthermore, may his mind be pure and single-minded, his four elements light and at ease, his life-span and wisdom-life extended, and his physical body and Dharma-body made firm. (Recite as appropriate.)

The Venerable Elder addressed the assembly on the night of his passing: "The Abbot has already returned to true stillness; the assembly has lost its reliance. One should simply contemplate impermanence and by no means be negligent.
Let us respectfully assemble and solemnly proceed to the funeral bier to recite the great names of the Buddhas, thereby providing spiritual support for the Venerable."
The Path of Spiritual Awakening. We rely upon the assembly to recite. Chant the Great Compassion Mantra.
May the merit of the above chanting and scripture-recitation assist the honored spirit and adorn their realm of retribution. We humbly pray that they may attain their wishes.
Next, the guest prefect shall receive the deceased’s fellow villagers and Dharma relatives. They shall ascend to offer incense and chant sutras at will.

[The funeral procession] proceeds to the coffin (the "constant" recitation is performed on the mountain peak). It is essential to note that by manifesting the sign of the double-legged posture, he inherited the legacy of Vulture Peak;

by returning to the West with his single sandal, he solemnly established the model of Shaolin. Through the full manifestation of his spiritual capacity, both hidden and revealed, he has brought the Dharma to its beginning and end. We rely upon the assembly for this.
Recite the Ten Buddhas (to assist the honored spirits in chanting the ten recitations of the West).

Having thus chanted the sacred names above, we reverently praise their transformative power. We pray that you embody the ultimate source of light and honor, so that your rank may suddenly transcend that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
that you may establish a model of conduct, and that your compassionate heart may reach all beings among humans and devas, gathering in the hundredfold marvels of illusory transformations.

Entering the Samādhi of the Blazing Fire, with three libations poured as the tea ebbs and a single incense burner incensed, we respectfully escort [the deceased] upon their journey through the clouds.
We prostrate to the assembly of noble ones. The Abbot and the senior monks chant for the distribution of robes.
Leaving behind robes as a token of faith is the established rule of our successive patriarchs; employing the Dharma to overcome stinginess follows the exemplary model of the former sages.
This current auction of the robes is intended to manifest impermanence. We rely upon the assembly to keep the robes in mind at every thought.

Once the chanting for the Buddhist service is concluded, we shall chant for the merit of the distribution of the robes. We humbly pray that this may assist the awakening spirit of [Name], adorning it...
The Ground of Retribution. Contemplate the ten directions and the three periods of time (etc.). Alternatively, contemplate and make vows according to one's wishes.

For the recitation during the Great Night of the Sangha (the term "Great Night" refers to the *vīnāya* who leads the recitation; when addressing them, use their two-character name, while for other dedications, use their single-character name).
It is essential to consider that life and death alternate and cold and heat shift in succession. Their coming is like a flash of lightning striking the vast sky; their departure is...
The waves clear the great ocean. This very day, [Name], who has recently entered parinirvāṇa, has reached the end of his life’s conditions; his great life has suddenly departed.

Having realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, he has found bliss in quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). We respectfully assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the reliquary chamber.
Silently reciting the sublime names of all Buddhas, I dedicate this pure spirit to the path of enlightenment. I respectfully rely upon the Great Assembly to recite:
"The Ten Buddhas of the Pure Dharma Body" (and so forth). [Recite the Sutra.]
The merit of the foregoing recitations and chanting of the sutras is respectfully offered to adorn the path to enlightenment for [Name].

We pray that their spirit may transcend to the pure realm and their karma be extinguished from the toils of the mundane world. May they bloom with the flowers of the highest grade and receive the prediction of Buddhahood within one lifetime.
(Recite again as before. [Lifting the coffin, reciting while departing the funeral procession.]
As we prepare to lift the sacred reliquary shrine for the grand ceremony of *tejovibhava* (cremation), we respectfully rely upon the venerable assembly to recite the great names of the Buddhas.
This serves as an expression of our longing and sorrow, and is offered to support the path to enlightenment through the practice of *buddhānusmṛti* (mindfulness of the Buddha) [and so forth].
On this day, [Name], who had recently passed into parinirvāṇa, followed conditions to enter peaceful extinction; we have thus performed the cremation according to the Dharma.
The body that practiced the Way for a hundred years has been consumed by fire, entering the realm of *nirvāṇa* on the single path. We rely upon your venerable presence...
Assembly, assist the awakening spirit by chanting the ten recitations.
Having thus chanted the holy names to assist those seeking rebirth, we pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the true breeze may disperse its splendor.
Within the Garden of Bodhi, the flowers of awakening-mind bloom; within the ocean of the Dharma-nature, the defilements of one’s own mind are washed away.
With three libations of tea poured and a single burner of incense lit, we respectfully escort you upon your journey through the clouds. Homage to the assembly of sages!
Recite the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī for the dedication of merit. As stated above, next recite the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī.

The *kāṣāya* is to be auctioned; chant the verses and strike the bell before the hall. Once the assembly has gathered and settled, the *raṇa* strikes the *qing* once and says: "As drifting clouds disperse, their shadows do not remain;
as the wick of the dying candle is spent, its light naturally extinguishes. This present auction is employed to manifest impermanence; we rely upon the venerable assembly."
Mindfulness. Ten Buddhas. [Striking the chime to address the assembly:
Now, as for the method of auctioning the robes, it follows established custom. You must take care regarding whether they are new or old, long or short.

The money must be full-value; do not attempt to combine it with new credit. Once the sound of the chime has ceased, no regrets shall be permitted. This is respectfully announced. The auction of the robes is concluded.

Then he says: "The aforementioned chanting of the *kāṣāya* and recitation of mantras for merit are dedicated to [the deceased] (Name), who has recently passed away, to assist their enlightened spirit in rebirth in the Pure Land.

Once again, I request the assembly to recite: 'To the Buddhas of the Ten Directions' (*etc.*). Having thus requested the funeral rites in advance, he strikes the gavel and conducts the inspection of the hall.
Outside the gate, firewood is distributed to the various funeral processions. Afterwards, the sutras are chanted; everything is as previously detailed.
Each performed their duties to the best of their ability, forming mutual karmic connections.

When a *śrāmaṇera* received the ordination, the ritual master first requested the *duò* (ordination certificate) on his behalf, placing it in a lined box to present to his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), as well as to the administrative officers and the heads of the community. Each...
Offer three prostrations in thanks. Select an auspicious day for the tonsure ceremony. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall issue the invitation.

For one receiving the precepts, the hair is shaved the night before, leaving only a tuft on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) to await the tonsure by the Preceptor (*ācārya*). On that day, in the Sangha Hall or the Dharma Hall, arrange and set up a high seat for the Preceptor.
Spread mats and rugs before it. Upon the incense altar, place an incense burner, a pure water flask, the text of the precepts (*śīla-sūtra*), and the two boundary markers (*sīmā-koṭaka*).
Article. Furthermore, facing the Preceptor (śikṣācārya), set up the seat for the Upādhyāya (karmācārya), along with one chime-bell (*kiṅkaṇī*), as if it were in the Dharma Hall.
There, separately install sacred images and offer incense and flowers. Set out three *zhaozi* (small stools) and a chest with a lid;

place the *kāṣāya* robe in one, the ordination certificate (*duòdié*) in another, and the ritual implements (*chēngzī*) in the third. Arrange these in front of the Sacred Monk or the sacred image. Below the hall, arrange the seats for prostration.

One mat. Once the preparations are complete, assemble the congregation. (If the ritual is performed to escort [the candidate], proceed from the Hall for Novices to the Hall of the Local Deity, then return to the Great Hall, and finally enter the Hall of Faith.

The novices who shave the head shall each perform three prostrations at their respective locations. The novices who shave the head shall immediately wait before the Sangha Hall until the assembly has settled.
After the Preceptor and the two Ācāryas have performed three full prostrations before the sacred image, the Preceptor performs the *brahman* chant while the Ācārya takes his place.

Having taken their seats, they enter into the ritual proceedings. They request the Preceptor for Invitation (to stand before the Preceptor of the Precepts, perform three prostrations with full prostration, and then kneel with palms joined).
The Preceptor (asks): "Is the Sangha assembled?

(Answer): "It is assembled. "Are you in harmony? (Answer): "We are in harmony. "The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall it do? (Answer): "To shave the head and confer the precepts upon the attendant of this monastery, [Name].
(Response): "So be it. The Preceptor (withdraws his sitting mat, rises, and leads the candidate into the hall).

The practitioner (before the noble Sangha, performs three prostrations. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing* bell, they prostrate; upon hearing the sound of the *qing* bell again, they rise and prostrate once more. They perform three prostrations before the Preceptor, then kneel with palms joined).
The Invoking of the Ācārya (reciting the *Upāli* *brahman*; if one cannot act as the teacher, recite the *kathaṃ-brahman*): "How shall one, regarding this sūtra, ultimately reach the other shore?

We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle and secret mysteries. (Chanting the incense mantra: May he preach it extensively for the sake of sentient beings; may he preach it for those who have shaved their heads and received the precepts."

The Preceptor (holding the incense burner while listening to the *brahman* voice, recites the mantra over the incense in a secluded place and fumigates it; the text for manifesting the precepts states: The fragrance of morality, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, and the fragrance of liberation.
The fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation; its clouds of radiant light pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Making offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, and being universally perfumed by seeing and hearing the infinite Dharmas and infinite Sanghas of the ten directions, one realizes eternal bliss. All sentient beings are likewise so.
The Preceptor (the Sanskrit term repeated) speaks for the one who has undergone tonsure and received the precepts. He now dedicates the merit of this morning’s tonsure and reception of the precepts:
may the Emperor live ten thousand years; may his ministers govern for a thousand autumns; may there be peace throughout the world; may the Wheel of Dharma turn perpetually;

may the dragons, devas, and local deities increase in majestic radiance; may they protect the Dharma and protect people, so that no calamities arise; and may all those in the ten directions [receive]... [offerings].

May the sovereign’s merit, longevity, and adornments flourish; may all those gathered at this *maṇḍala* site find peace and joy in body and mind; may teachers and parents excel in their spiritual endeavors;

may the novice monks who have shaved their heads encounter no obstacles in their practice; may all beings in the three miserable realms and eight difficult conditions be liberated from the wheel of suffering;

and may all those within the nine states of existence and four modes of birth ascend together to the shore of enlightenment. We look up with reverence to the venerable assembly and invoke the pure *dharmakāya* (and so forth)... until *mahāparinirvāṇa*.

If it is a *pāramitā* [ordination], one invites the *ācārya* (holding the incense burner, the words for the invitation should be recited by the candidate themselves; if they are unable, follow my voice). [At the point of "at such-and-such field," state the name. "Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [Name], now request the Virtuous One to act as my *ācārya* for the shaving of the head and the reception of the precepts."

"Venerable Sir, it is by relying upon you that I have been able to shave my head and receive the precepts. Out of compassion, [please do so]—(so stated three times; on the third repetition, 'out of compassion,' three times)."
The practitioner (for the first, second, and third [times], each performs three minor prostrations; then again three prostrations and three bows, kneeling with palms joined).

"Good son" (each time he calls "good son," one should respond with an assent). "The source of the world is profound stillness; the ocean of Dharma is deep and vast. Those who are deluded therein will sink and drift for eternal kalpas; those who awaken to it shall attain liberation in this very place.
If you wish to devote yourself exclusively to the wondrous Way, there is nothing that surpasses leaving the household life. To be free and expansive..."
It is like empty space; pure and clear as the bright moon. When the conditions for cultivation are complete, the fruit of the Way is not far off.

Beginning with the merit of moment-to-moment mindfulness, one ultimately realizes the stage of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One renounced his precious throne of the Golden Wheel and, at the hour of midnight, crossed the city walls.
He cast off his precious dragon-robe and cut his hair on the green mountains, allowing a magpie’s nest to remain upon his head.

Atop his head, he hangs a spiderweb across his brow; by cultivating cessation (*śamatha*), he realizes the true and eternal, and by severing worldly toil (*kleśa*), he attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Among the Buddhas of the three periods of time, none are said to have attained the Way while remaining a householder. Among the six generations of patriarchs, who ever practiced defilement to save others?

Therefore, from Buddha to Buddha there is the passing of the hand, and from patriarch to patriarch there is the transmission: only by remaining unstained by worldly conditions does one become a vessel for the Dharma.
Thus, the celestial Māra stood with hands folded in submission and the non-Buddhists turned their hearts toward the Way. Above, he repaid the fourfold debt of gratitude;

below, he rescued sentient beings from their suffering. Therefore it is said: "While wandering through the three realms, one cannot abandon affectionate ties; by casting aside such ties, one enters the unconditioned."
Truly, you are one who repays kindness. After leaving the household life, your conduct transcends ordinary custom: you do not bow to kings, nor do you bow to your parents.

You may now leave this seat; while reflecting upon the King’s grace in providing the land and water, and your parents’ virtue in giving you birth and life, perform your prostrations with single-minded devotion as a formal farewell, for thereafter you shall no longer bow.
The Preceptor (ācārya) who leads the invitation [rises from his seat, folds his sitting cloth, and rises; he and the practitioner perform mutual greetings and exit the hall].

The practitioner [at the foot of the hall, bows in farewell to the King, parents, and relatives; having inspected his secular clothing and donned the *zhiduo* robe, he follows the Preceptor who leads the invitation. They proceed before the sacred image and perform three prostrations. Then, [the practitioner] takes his place at the seat of the Preceptor;
after one prostration and one bow, he approaches, kneels with his right knee on the ground (*hu-kuei*), and joins his palms].
The Preceptor (recites the verse while holding a flask of water to pour over the head and shaving a small amount of hair; the monks standing nearby recite along with him): Excellent, O Great Man!
You are able to realize the impermanence of the world. Abandoning the secular life to seek Nirvāṇa—this is rare and inconceivable.
(Recite three times. The Śrāmaṇera withdraws and performs one prostration.)
The Preceptor (the officiant) invites [the candidate] (the candidate prostrates once before the Preceptor’s seat, approaches, and kneels with palms joined).
The Preceptor holds a razor and says: "This final knot is called the *cūḍā*; only a Buddha alone is able to sever it.
I shall now remove the hair from your crown for you; do you consent? The candidate replies: "So be it. The Preceptor says:
Look up to the great assembly and recite the verse for shaving the hair in unison:
Destroying the form to preserve the will and integrity, Severing attachment to bid farewell to kin, Leaving home to propagate the Holy Way, I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
(Recite three times. [Withdraw from the assembly. Prostrate once. Return before the Master, kneeling with palms joined.]
The Preceptor, holding the *kāṣāya*, recites the verse:

"How great is this robe of liberation! The signless field of merit garment. Donning it to uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts, I shall extensively deliver all sentient beings. (Recite this once and bestow it upon him.)

Once the śrāmaṇera has finished donning the kāṣāya, he prostrates three times to his preceptor, three times to the sacred image, and three times to the preceptor of the precepts; then he kneels with his right knee on the ground and joins his palms.
The Preceptor (Ācārya) invites [the candidate] (also spreading his sitting mat, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms):

"O son of good family, the Dharma is like a great ocean; one enters it gradually and becomes increasingly deep. Now that you have left the household life, you must first receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before you may attend upon the Great Sangha.
Next, you shall receive the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, whereupon you may partake in the benefits and offerings shared by the Sangha."

The matter lies in single-minded sincerity; one should not be negligent or casual. I now invoke the Triple Gem on your behalf to bear witness to this Buddhist rite (furthermore, with the intent of the ten precepts).

We reverently entreat the boundless ocean-treasury of the Buddha-jewels—the Ten Grounds, the Three Sages, the Five Fruits, and the Four Approaches—to descend together in response to our invocation and collectively act as witnesses. (Recite three times.)
"Good son, if you wish to seek refuge and receive the precepts, you must first repent and cleanse your transgressions and defects. It is like a person who washes their clothes before applying dye.
You should now, with utmost sincerity, follow me in repentance."
All the evil karmas I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I now confess them all.
Good son, since you have thus purified the karma of body, speech, and mind, you should next take refuge in the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
I take refuge in the Buddha. I take refuge in the Dharma. I take refuge in the Saṅgha. I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire. I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among assemblies.
Taking refuge in the Buddha is complete. Taking refuge in the Dharma is complete. Taking refuge in the Saṅgha is complete.
The Tathāgata, the Most Honored One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my teacher; I now take refuge in him.

From this day forward, I shall call the Buddha my teacher and will no longer take refuge in demons, heretics, or outsiders. Out of compassion (recite three times; on the third repetition, say "out of compassion" three times).
The Śrāmaṇera (first, second, and third [times]: each performs one small prostration and three great prostrations, kneeling with palms joined).

"Good son, since you have abandoned the heterodox and returned to the orthodox, and your precepts are now complete, if you wish to recognize the characteristics of the precepts and maintain them, you should receive the five precepts."
For as long as life lasts, one shall observe the precepts of refraining from killing and refraining from stealing.
Abstaining from sexual misconduct,
abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from intoxicants.
"These are the characteristics of the five precepts. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them.
"Regarding these aforementioned five branches of pure precepts, you must not violate even one. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them. (Three questions and three answers.
"In this manner, you shall uphold them."
The śrāmaṇera (performs three prostrations with great ceremony, kneels with the right knee on the ground, and joins his palms).
"Good son, the five precepts are the beginning of entry into the Dharma; they are the primary means for emerging from the three miserable realms.

Next, one receives the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, whereby one’s physical form becomes fully endowed with the ritual requirements of the Dharma. This is called a 'diligent restrainer' (śikṣamāṇa). One dwells in reliance upon a teacher and receives benefits equal to those of the monastic community."
This is what constitutes a śrāmaṇera who accords with the Dharma; you should receive this upon the crown of your head and observe it for as long as life lasts:
abstaining from taking life, abstaining from flower garlands, necklaces, and perfumed oils for anointing the body.
One does not steal; one does not go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or musical performances;
one does not engage in sexual misconduct; one does not sit or lie on high, wide, or large beds;
one does not speak falsehoods; and one does not eat at improper times.
Not drinking alcohol, and not handling gold, silver, money, or treasures—these ten matters above are the śrāmaṇera precepts. Are you able to uphold them? (He replies: I am able to uphold them.

Regarding the ten branches of pure precepts mentioned above, not one may be transgressed. Are you able to uphold them? (He answers: "I am able to uphold them. (The question is asked three times and the answer given three times.
Thus shall this matter be upheld.
The śrāmaṇera (performs three prostrations with the Great Rite; kneels on the right knee with palms joined):
"O son of good family, after you have now received the precepts, you must uphold them with the highest reverence. You must not violate the precepts you have undertaken.
You shall make offerings to the Triple Gem, diligently cultivate the field of merit, and treat your upādhyāya and ācārya exactly according to the Dharma."
As for the teachings: toward seniors, those of middle rank, and juniors, one should always maintain a mind of reverence. Practice the Way with diligent effort to repay the kindness of one's parents.

For clothing, take plain cloth rather than dyed or patterned fabrics; for food, take what sustains life rather than indulging in flavors. Let flowers, incense, cosmetics, and powders not come near the body.
As for pleasant sounds and seductive sights, do not look upon or listen to them at all. Speak slowly and maintain rectitude; do not proclaim the shortcomings of others. Should there be...
As for "contention": it is the reconciliation of two opposing views. There is distinction between male and female; there is no harm to plants or trees.

One does not befriend those who are not virtuous, nor does one revere those who are not sages. Dharma-robes and alms-bowls are always kept with one. One does not eat at improper times and does not speak what is not in accordance with the Dharma.

Diligently applying oneself to contemplate the meaning, one reviews the old to know the new. When seated, one practices meditative contemplation; when rising, one recites the scriptures. Thus, the three evil realms are closed off and Nirvana is opened.
Within the dharma of the bhikṣu, he increases right action; his bodhicitta does not regress, and his prajñā-wisdom remains perpetually luminous.
Universally delivering sentient beings, he aspires to achieve perfect enlightenment. One who applies the mind in this way is a true disciple of the Buddha.
The Brahman Ācārya (the term *brahman* refers to a celestial being or immortal) is one who possesses the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Regarding those who practice incantations and spells, for the sake of those who possess a sense of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*), and to restrain those who lack such shame, the Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*). He proclaimed them every half-month.
Having explained the benefits of these precepts, I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas.

The Preceptor (holding the incense burner while reciting the *Brahma-svara* [Sanskrit] verses until their conclusion, then performs the dedication): The tonsure and reception of the precepts performed above are first dedicated as follows:
May the Abbot, the Head Monk, eternally serve as a bridge and raft across the sea of suffering; may the eminent officials and attendants forever act as the pillars and beams of the Dharma-gate;

may the pure assembly of the entire hall together board the vessel of Prajñā; and may the novice monk who has had his head shaved swiftly reach the shore of Bodhi. [Dedication for] the Four Debts of Gratitude...

As a collective retribution, may all beings throughout the three realms of existence be equally sustained, so that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm may together realize the omniscient wisdom (sarvajñā). For these aforementioned reasons,
I call to mind all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as all honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
Acting as the Brahma Preceptor, he strikes the chime and says: "Abiding in the world like space, Like a lotus flower, unsullied by water, The mind is pure and transcends that;
I prostrate and pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One."
I take refuge in the Buddha; may I attain Bodhi, and my resolve for the Way never regress.
I take refuge in the Dharma; may I attain the gate of great *dhāraṇī* through *prajñā*.
I take refuge in the Saṃgha; may disputes cease, and we together enter the ocean of harmony.

The aforementioned shaving of the head and receiving of the precepts constitute boundless merit and a most excellent, virtuous cause, which shall be dispersed throughout the entire *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.

I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. [The Preceptor] leads the way to invite the *ācārya* (upon hearing this, the disciple withdraws his sitting mat, rises, and causes the śrāmaṇera to prostrate).
The Preceptor of the Precepts (Jieshi), together with the *ācārya*, performs three full prostrations before the sacred image. They then exit the hall and stand before the Sangha Hall.

The small bell is struck three times, and the assembly descends from the hall. Each member assumes their proper dignified demeanor and pays respects to congratulate the Abbot on the Dharma Hall (*fatang*).
(If the tonsure ceremony takes place within the Dharma Hall, the congratulations are performed inside the Dharma Hall.)

The Preceptor and two Ācāryas: (First, having been appointed by the assembly to confer the precepts, I dare not firmly decline. Entering into this matter, I have been delayed for some time due to my lack of respect; my humble feelings are filled with the utmost awe and trepidation. Once again, [I] prostrate three times to express greetings regarding the season’s cold or heat.

I humbly wish that the Venerable Master’s health and daily life be blessed with ten thousand blessings. Thereupon, one again performs three prostrations. The Abbot says: "Regarding the novice monk’s reception of the precepts, I have troubled you to serve as witnesses; please allow me to go to the quarters to offer my thanks.

The Attendant and junior disciples perform a congratulatory ceremony: (They perform three full prostrations and say: "That the novice has attained ordination is a joy shared by the entire assembly. Facing your venerable kindness, our hearts leap with double the delight. Again, three prostrations to express greetings regarding the season’s cold or heat."

[The officiant] performs three prostrations. The administrative officers and the assembly return to their quarters. Each person prepares incense and stands in a single file. They wait; at that moment, as soon as the assembly has withdrawn, the śrāmaṇeras perform three prostrations [saying]:

"By receiving this topknot, we have fortunately donned the field-cloth robes. Thus we have escaped the prison of dust and forever cast off the net of sorrow. We, your humble servants, are moved beyond measure by this profound gratitude. They perform three prostrations to exchange greetings, then another three prostrations.

The Abbot then visits the quarters in turn and performs prostrations [to the following]: the administrative officers, the head monks, the preceptors, the ācāryas, and all fellow dharma-kinsmen. The Words of Thanks for the Great Precepts: "Ten-thousand-year reign! By the grace of Heaven..."

The auspicious season has dawned; the three recitations at the Frost Terrace have been completed. As the *karmavācanā* is finalized, you have now ascended to the stage of the Precepts. This is surely because such-and-such a person, having long ago received the Buddha’s prophecy, vowed to deliver all deluded beings. Now, with a mind as steadfast as binding grass, they shall repay the gift of the life-raft above, and express their boundless gratitude below.
(I am overwhelmed by the utmost emotion.)

Next, having finished striking the meal-bell for the deceased *karmadāna* throughout its full cycle, strike it once more and say: "Informing the assembly: after the gruel, there is a general invitation to escort the deceased."

The monks, with the exception of those guarding the quarters and the hall, shall all attend the meal. Furthermore, strike the mallet once and announce: "I respectfully inform you that the inspection of the hall has been completed inside and out.

Once the preparations are finished, strike the bell to assemble the assembly. After the recitation and dedication of merit are complete, offer incense at the altar and perform the ritual for raising the coffin.
Next, stand in the center before the gate; as the sutra is chanted, the assembly divides into two groups and proceeds on either side, holding [the banners].
The procedure for the wooden shrine, the subsequent funeral rites, and other matters is as detailed previously.
Upon receiving the full precepts (Upasampadā), one returns to the Sangha hall;

when the long board (for the meal) sounds, one enters the gate and burns incense, performing three prostrations with the sitting cloth (niṣīdana) still unfurled. Advancing forward with a bowed body, one says: "I, [Name]..."
I, [Name], have by sheer fortune encountered the Sage’s grace and been permitted to join the ranks of the Sangha. Fortunate indeed that my precepts are now fully perfected;

I rely upon the pervasive protection of your compassionate influence. My humble heart is moved beyond measure with gratitude. [He] withdraws to perform three prostrations, then steps forward again and says:

"At this auspicious moment, I humbly wish the Head Seat, the Great Assembly, and the Chan Master ten thousand blessings. Having performed another three prostrations, he rises and proceeds before the Abbot.
Having circumambulated the hall once, proceed next to the Hall Office (Tangsi) to register for lodging.
